nodes.findings: Over 21 topics and 45 runs, run-level Kendall tau between automatic and (mostly) manual evaluation is 0.783; per-topic tau is 0.518, reliable for ranking systems but noisy per topic.
nodes.limitations: Per-topic agreement is noisy (tau 0.518); published as a TREC track report rather than a peer-reviewed paper.

nodes.label: Voorhees 2000 (assessor variation)
nodes.summary: Absolute retrieval scores shift with the assessor, but relative system orderings are stable across assessors' qrels (Kendall tau ~0.94).
nodes.significance: Foundational demonstration that absolute retrieval scores shift with the assessor while relative system orderings remain stable across assessors' qrels, licensing comparative evaluation based on pooling and a single consistent assessor.
nodes.findings: Relative system orderings are stable across different assessors' qrels at Kendall tau of approximately 0.94, despite shifts in absolute scores.

nodes.label: Don't use LLMs for relevance judgments
nodes.summary: Position: LLM-authored truth data collapses retrieval and evaluation into one problem and sets that LLM as a performance ceiling; LLMs may assist but final judgments should stay human-grounded.
nodes.significance: Position paper arguing that LLM-authored relevance judgments collapse retrieval and evaluation into a single problem and set the judging LLM as a performance ceiling; LLMs may assist with drafting and prioritizing, but final judgments should remain human-grounded and LLM-derived collections should not be labeled ground truth.

nodes.label: LLM judgments can't replace humans
nodes.summary: Critique of LLM relevance assessment: circularity (LLM judges can favor systems built on similar LLMs), leaderboard correlation is insufficient validity evidence, prompt sensitivity.
nodes.significance: Critique of LLM-based relevance assessment highlighting circularity (LLM judges can favor systems built on similar LLMs), the insufficiency of leaderboard correlation as validity evidence, and prompt sensitivity.
nodes.limitations: arXiv-only preprint; venue beyond arXiv unverified.

nodes.label: BM25 monograph (Robertson & Zaragoza)
nodes.summary: Canonical modern statement of BM25/BM25F derived from the probabilistic relevance framework.
nodes.significance: The canonical modern statement of BM25 and BM25F, derived from the probabilistic relevance framework. It remains the standard reference for sparse lexical ranking, which is a robust baseline in entity- and terminology-heavy domains where exact-match signals dominate.

nodes.label: BEIR
nodes.summary: Zero-shot heterogeneous retrieval benchmark (18 datasets): BM25 is a robust OOD baseline, dense models often underperform it out of domain, cross-encoders generalize best; in-domain rank does not predict transfer. No parliamentary collection exists in it.
nodes.significance: The standard heterogeneous benchmark for zero-shot retrieval evaluation, which reshaped how retrieval systems are compared across domains. Its central lessons — include a lexical baseline, and never assume in-domain rank predicts out-of-domain transfer — govern the design of any domain-specific retrieval evaluation; it also contains no parliamentary collection, confirming that gap.
nodes.findings: Across 18 datasets and 10 retrieval architectures evaluated zero-shot: BM25 is a robust out-of-domain baseline that many dense bi-encoders underperform (while losing 7-18 points in-domain on MS MARCO); cross-encoder rerankers generalize best at higher compute; in-domain performance does not predict zero-shot generalization.
nodes.limitations: Contains no parliamentary or political retrieval collection, so conclusions for that domain must be extrapolated from the nearest neighbors (news, scientific, financial datasets).

nodes.label: EntityQuestions (Sciavolino et al.)
nodes.summary: Simple entity-centric questions make dense retrievers (DPR) drastically underperform BM25; dense models generalize only to common entities.
nodes.significance: The most direct evidence that dense retrievers systematically fail on simple entity-centric queries where lexical matching excels. This failure mode is a core argument for hybrid or entity-aware retrieval in any domain whose queries revolve around named entities.
nodes.findings: On EntityQuestions (Wikidata-derived entity-centric questions), dense retrievers such as DPR drastically underperform BM25; dense models generalize only to common entities seen in training distributions.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG, whose queries are heavily entity-centric (deputies, parties, bills, ministries) and therefore directly exposed to this dense-retrieval failure mode.

nodes.label: DPR (Karpukhin et al.)
nodes.summary: Dual-encoder trained with in-batch negatives beats BM25 by 9-19 points top-20 accuracy on open QA; established dense retrieval as practical.
nodes.significance: The paper that established dense passage retrieval as practical: a dual encoder trained with in-batch negatives beating BM25 on open-domain QA. It is the origin of the bi-encoder architecture underlying most modern dense retrieval channels, and the starting point of the arc (DPR, BEIR, EntityQuestions) showing dense-only retrieval is not sufficient.
nodes.findings: The dual encoder with in-batch negatives beats BM25 by 9-19 points top-20 retrieval accuracy on open-domain QA benchmarks.
nodes.limitations: Its BM25 baseline was later shown to be under-tuned and the effectiveness of dense+sparse hybrids under-reported (Ma et al. 2021); subsequent work documented poor generalization to rare entities and out-of-domain collections.

nodes.label: Sentence-BERT
nodes.summary: Siamese/triplet fine-tuning makes BERT embeddings cosine-comparable; the recipe (pooling + contrastive fine-tuning) that turns any MLM into a retriever.
nodes.significance: Established that siamese/triplet fine-tuning with pooling turns BERT into a usable sentence embedder with cosine-comparable vectors. It defines the recipe by which any MLM encoder, including domain-adapted ones, must be converted before it can serve as a retriever.
nodes.findings: Siamese and triplet fine-tuning makes BERT sentence embeddings cosine-comparable, becoming the template for sentence-embedding-based retrieval and the basis of the sentence-transformers ecosystem.

nodes.label: DPR replication (hybrid evidence)
nodes.summary: DPR's BM25 baseline was under-tuned; with a proper baseline, an alpha-weighted dense+BM25 hybrid consistently beats both single channels.
nodes.significance: A replication study showing that DPR's original BM25 baseline was under-tuned, and that a properly tuned sparse baseline plus a simple alpha-weighted dense+BM25 interpolation consistently beats either channel alone. It supplies both the corrected evidence for hybrid retrieval and the simplest hybrid scoring form to compare against rank fusion.
nodes.findings: With a properly tuned BM25 baseline, the hybrid s_dense + alpha*BM25 consistently outperforms both single channels across all tested settings; hybrid effectiveness was understated in the original DPR paper.
nodes.limitations: arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed.

nodes.label: Fusion function analysis (Bruch et al.)
nodes.summary: Systematic comparison of convex score combination vs RRF: a tuned convex combination outperforms RRF in- and out-of-domain, and is robust to normalization choice.
nodes.significance: The key modern analysis of fusion functions for hybrid retrieval, showing that a tuned convex combination of scores outperforms reciprocal rank fusion both in- and out-of-domain. It rehabilitates score-level convex fusion against the widespread default of RRF, provided the weights are actually tuned.
nodes.findings: A tuned convex score combination outperforms RRF in-domain and out-of-domain and is largely robust to the choice of score normalization; RRF is more sensitive to its parameters than commonly assumed.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: it defends a convex weighted merger over RRF, but only if the fusion weights are tuned rather than expert-set.

nodes.label: Dense retrievers require BM25 interpolation
nodes.summary: Dense retrievers encode strong relevance signals but miss weaker ones; BM25 interpolation recovers them with significant gains, unlike for rerankers.
nodes.significance: Shows that dense retrievers capture strong relevance signals but miss weaker ones, and that interpolation with BM25 recovers them — a complementarity result explaining why hybrid gains concentrate in the mid-rank region. It also shows the same interpolation is unnecessary for cross-encoder rerankers.
nodes.findings: Dense retrievers encode strong relevance signals but miss weaker ones; BM25 interpolation recovers them with significant gains, whereas BERT rerankers do not require interpolation.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: it predicts BM25 adds most value in the mid-rank region, exactly where balance quotas draw additional evidence from.

nodes.label: Sparse, dense, attentional representations
nodes.summary: Theory: fixed-length dense encodings have capacity limits growing with document length; sparse-dense hybrids capture sparse precision plus dense recall.
nodes.significance: Provides the theoretical account of why fixed-length dense encodings have capacity limits that grow with document length and required ranking margin, and why sparse-dense hybrids combining lexical precision with dense recall outperform either representation. It grounds both hybrid retrieval and the practice of embedding at passage rather than document level.
nodes.findings: Theoretically and empirically, fixed-length dense encodings hit capacity limits as document length and required ranking margin grow; sparse-dense hybrids capture sparse precision plus dense recall and outperform both single representations.

nodes.label: CombSUM/CombMNZ (Fox & Shaw)
nodes.summary: Introduced CombSUM (sum of normalized scores) and CombMNZ: the origin of score-level fusion.
nodes.significance: The origin of score-level fusion in information retrieval, introducing CombSUM and CombMNZ. Weighted score-combination mergers used in modern multi-channel retrieval systems descend from this family rather than from rank-based fusion.
nodes.findings: Introduced CombSUM (sum of normalized scores across systems) and CombMNZ (CombSUM multiplied by the number of systems retrieving the document), establishing score-level combination of multiple searches.

nodes.label: Reciprocal Rank Fusion
nodes.summary: RRF score = sum over rankings of 1/(k + rank), k=60; rank-based, scale-free fusion that beat every individual system and Condorcet fusion on TREC runs.
nodes.significance: Introduced Reciprocal Rank Fusion, the rank-based, scale-free, parameter-light fusion method that became the de facto standard for combining retrieval channels without score calibration. It is the natural baseline against which any bespoke fusion design must be compared.
nodes.findings: RRF scores documents as the sum over rankings of 1/(k + rank) with k=60 chosen in a pilot study; fusing TREC runs and learning-to-rank outputs, it beat every individual system and Condorcet fusion.
nodes.limitations: Being purely rank-based, RRF cannot exploit score magnitudes or express non-relevance objectives such as coverage or diversity; later analysis (Bruch et al. 2023) found tuned convex score combinations outperform it.

nodes.label: MMR (Carbonell & Goldstein)
nodes.summary: Maximal Marginal Relevance: greedy selection trading query relevance against redundancy with already-selected items.
nodes.significance: Introduced Maximal Marginal Relevance, the greedy selection criterion trading query relevance against redundancy with already-selected items. It is the ancestor of virtually all diversity-aware ranking and redundancy-penalizing selection mechanisms, in retrieval and in extractive summarization.
nodes.findings: Defined MMR as greedy selection maximizing a convex combination of query similarity and negative maximum similarity to already-selected items, applied to document reordering and summary construction.

nodes.label: xQuAD (Santos et al.)
nodes.summary: Explicit diversification: model the query's aspects and greedily maximize coverage of uncovered aspects, versus MMR's implicit dissimilarity.
nodes.significance: Introduced xQuAD, the explicit diversification framework that models a query's aspects and greedily maximizes coverage of aspects not yet covered, in contrast to MMR's implicit content dissimilarity. It is the conceptual home of diversification schemes whose aspects are known a priori, such as coverage constraints over exogenous categories.
nodes.findings: Explicit aspect-based diversification via query reformulations outperforms implicit dissimilarity-based approaches for web search result diversification.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: per-party quotas are explicit diversification over exogenous known aspects (the party system), and party-coverage metrics are aspect-recall analogues.

nodes.label: HyDE (Gao et al.)
nodes.summary: LLM generates a hypothetical answer document whose embedding retrieves real documents; gains demonstrated zero-shot with unsupervised encoders, shrinking with stronger retrievers.
nodes.significance: Introduced hypothetical document embeddings: an LLM generates a hypothetical answer document whose embedding retrieves real documents via document-document similarity. It became a widely adopted zero-shot retrieval technique, though the paper itself frames it as a substitute for relevance supervision rather than a universal add-on.
nodes.findings: Zero-shot gains are demonstrated with unsupervised encoders (Contriever); the paper shows the margin over fine-tuned or stronger retrievers shrinks.
nodes.limitations: Gains diminish or reverse for strong in-domain retrievers, and hallucinated hypothetical documents can inject wrong entities or framings into the query representation.

nodes.label: When do expansions fail?
nodes.authors: Weller, Lo, Wadden, Lawrie & Van Durme
nodes.summary: Across 11 expansion techniques x 24 retrievers x 12 datasets: strong negative correlation between retriever strength and expansion gains; expansion generally harms strong models.
nodes.significance: The pivotal large-scale study of when generative query and document expansion fails, establishing that expansion benefits are inversely related to retriever strength. It provides the central evidence-based prior against adding LLM expansion (HyDE, multi-query) on top of strong retrievers.
nodes.findings: Across 11 expansion techniques, 24 retrievers, and 12 datasets, there is a strong negative correlation between retriever strength and expansion gains: expansion helps weak models and generally harms strong ones, dropping precision at the top of the ranking even when recall rises.

nodes.label: monoT5 reranking
nodes.summary: T5 generates true/false as relevance; strong zero-shot cross-domain reranking, robust in low-data and legal settings.
nodes.significance: Established sequence-to-sequence reranking, with T5 generating a true/false relevance token, as a strong zero-shot cross-domain reranker that is notably robust in low-data and legal settings. It is the ancestor of the practical multilingual cross-encoder rerankers used in production retrieval pipelines.
nodes.findings: monoT5 achieves strong zero-shot cross-domain reranking effectiveness and is robust in low-data and legal-domain settings.

nodes.label: RankGPT
nodes.summary: Listwise permutation-generation reranking with GPT-3.5/4 beats fine-tuned cross-encoders zero-shot; permutation distillation into a 440M model outperforms a 3B supervised model.
nodes.significance: Showed that listwise permutation-generation reranking with large LLMs beats fine-tuned cross-encoders zero-shot, and that this capability can be distilled into small models. It defines the quality upper bound for reranking and the distillation route to deployable rerankers.
nodes.findings: Listwise permutation-generation reranking with GPT-3.5/4 beats fine-tuned cross-encoders zero-shot on BEIR/TREC; permutation distillation into a 440M-parameter model outperforms a 3B supervised model.
nodes.limitations: Requires many LLM calls per query, giving latency and cost profiles incompatible with interactive, streaming, or high-volume serving.

nodes.label: GraphRAG (Microsoft)
nodes.summary: LLM-extracted entity graph + community summaries for global sensemaking queries; evaluation is LLM-judge head-to-head with no standard IR metrics.
nodes.significance: The most-cited graph-RAG reference: an LLM-extracted entity graph with community detection and community summaries used to answer global sensemaking queries over a corpus. Its evidentiary status is weak — unreviewed and evaluated only by LLM-judge head-to-head comparisons — and its graph quality depends on noisy LLM extraction, in contrast to approaches that traverse curated institutional structure.
nodes.findings: LLM-extracted entity graphs with community summaries improve responses to global, query-focused summarization questions in LLM-as-judge head-to-head evaluations.
nodes.limitations: Not peer-reviewed; evaluation is LLM-as-judge only with no standard IR metrics; the graph is built by LLM extraction and inherits its noise.

nodes.label: HippoRAG
nodes.summary: OpenIE-built KG + Personalized PageRank seeded by query entities for single-step multi-hop retrieval; up to 20% better on multi-hop QA at 10-20x lower cost.
nodes.significance: The peer-reviewed anchor for graph-augmented retrieval: an OpenIE-built knowledge graph with Personalized PageRank seeded by query entities enables single-step multi-hop retrieval. It provides the strongest published evidence that entity-graph traversal complements dense retrieval, and PPR offers a soft, weighted alternative to fixed-depth graph traversal.
nodes.findings: Achieves up to 20% better performance on multi-hop QA than iterative retrieval methods at 10-20x lower cost, and combines productively with dense retrieval.

nodes.label: BM25 strong in legal retrieval
nodes.summary: Vanilla BM25 placed 2nd in COLIEE 2021 case retrieval, above nearly all neural submissions; the broader pattern holds across legal corpora.
nodes.significance: Demonstrated that vanilla BM25 remains a top competitor in legal case retrieval, outperforming nearly all neural submissions in COLIEE 2021. It is the strongest domain-transfer prior that lexical retrieval excels on formal, citation- and terminology-heavy text such as legal and parliamentary language.
nodes.findings: Vanilla BM25 placed 2nd in COLIEE 2021 case retrieval, above nearly all neural submissions; the broader pattern of BM25 robustness holds across legal corpora and under temporal drift.
nodes.limitations: Competition report published only on arXiv, not journal-reviewed.

nodes.label: LegalBench-RAG
nodes.summary: 6,858 QA pairs over 700+ contracts with precise citation-span annotations, built to evaluate the retrieval component of legal RAG separately from generation.
nodes.significance: A benchmark built specifically to evaluate the retrieval component of legal RAG separately from generation, using precise citation-span annotations over contracts. It is the methodological template for constructing domain-specific retrieval test collections with span-level relevance decoupled from end-to-end generation quality.
nodes.findings: Provides 6,858 QA pairs over 700+ contracts with precise citation-span annotations, enabling retrieval-only evaluation of legal RAG systems.
nodes.limitations: Preprint, not peer-reviewed; covers contracts, a register distinct from legislative or parliamentary text, so the design rather than the data transfers to other domains.

nodes.label: Don't Stop Pretraining (DAPT)
nodes.summary: Domain-adaptive and task-adaptive continued pretraining yield consistent classification gains across 4 domains and 8 tasks; gains largest for distant domains.
nodes.significance: The canonical work on domain-adaptive and task-adaptive continued pretraining, showing consistent downstream gains across domains and resource settings. It is the standard justification for building domain-adapted encoders, with the important caveat that all its evidence concerns classification rather than retrieval or sentence embeddings.
nodes.findings: DAPT and TAPT on RoBERTa yield consistent gains across 4 domains and 8 classification tasks in both high- and low-resource settings; TAPT helps even after DAPT; gains are largest when the target domain is distant from the pretraining distribution.
nodes.limitations: All downstream evidence is classification, not retrieval or sentence embeddings; the study says nothing about the geometry of pooled sentence vectors.

nodes.label: CaseHOLD (When does pretraining help?)
nodes.summary: Legal DAPT gains appear only on difficult, highly domain-specific tasks (+7.2 F1 on CaseHOLD); gains scale with task difficulty times domain specificity.
nodes.significance: Refined the DAPT picture by showing that domain-pretraining gains appear only on difficult, highly domain-specific tasks, explaining earlier null results on easy legal benchmarks. It predicts that domain adaptation pays off only when the evaluation genuinely stresses domain-specific semantics, motivating hard register-specific test queries.
nodes.findings: A custom legal-corpus-pretrained BERT gains +7.2 F1 over generic BERT on the new, difficult CaseHOLD task; gains scale with task difficulty times domain specificity, while easy legal tasks show few DAPT gains.

nodes.label: LEGAL-BERT
nodes.summary: Legal-domain BERT variants beat vanilla BERT on domain tasks, but gains are modest and dataset-dependent; scratch vs continued pretraining mostly comparable.
nodes.significance: The template for a domain-encoder release in the legal domain, comparing from-scratch and continued pretraining on large legal corpora. It also serves as tempering evidence: domain gains were real but modest and dataset-dependent, and evaluation covered only classification and NER, never retrieval.
nodes.findings: BERT variants pretrained on ~12 GB of legal text beat vanilla BERT on legal downstream tasks, but gains are modest and dataset-dependent; from-scratch and continued pretraining perform mostly comparably, and standard pretrain/fine-tune guidelines do not always generalize to the legal domain.
nodes.limitations: Evaluated only on classification and NER tasks; no retrieval or sentence-embedding evaluation.

nodes.label: ITALIAN-LEGAL-BERT
nodes.summary: Continued pretraining of Italian BERT on Italian civil-law corpora, evaluated on Italian legal downstream tasks.
nodes.significance: A domain-adapted BERT for Italian law, built by continued pretraining of Italian BERT on civil-law corpora and evaluated on Italian legal downstream tasks. It shows the Italian NLP ecosystem produces domain encoders for the register closest to parliamentary Italian (formal, procedural, entity-heavy), while no parliamentary equivalent exists for Italian.

nodes.label: PoliBERTweet
nodes.summary: BERTweet continued-pretrained on 83M US-election tweets; outperforms general LMs on political downstream tasks including stance detection.
nodes.significance: The main political-domain pretrained encoder in the literature: BERTweet continued-pretrained on a large corpus of US-election tweets, outperforming general-purpose language models on political downstream tasks. It repeats the evidence pattern of political/parliamentary DAPT models: gains on classification and stance tasks, with no retrieval or embedding evaluation.
nodes.findings: BERTweet continued-pretrained on 83M US-election tweets outperforms general-purpose language models on political downstream tasks, including candidate stance detection.
nodes.limitations: Evaluated only on classification and stance tasks; no retrieval or sentence-embedding evaluation; restricted to the social-media register.

nodes.label: ParlBERT-German / FrameASt
nodes.summary: GermanBERT continued-pretrained on German parliamentary debates (v2 on >30M political sentences from GerParCor); used for CAP topic classification.
nodes.significance: The German parliamentary DAPT encoder: GermanBERT continued-pretrained on parliamentary debates (v2 on more than 30M political sentences from GerParCor) and applied to Comparative Agendas Project topic classification. It confirms the pattern that parliamentary DAPT encoders exist across languages but are evaluated only on classification, never retrieval.
nodes.findings: GermanBERT continued-pretrained on German parliamentary debates (v2 on >30M political sentences from GerParCor) was applied to CAP topic classification of parliamentary debates within the FrameASt framework.
nodes.limitations: Evaluated only on topic classification; no retrieval or sentence-embedding evaluation.

nodes.label: ParlaSent multilingual / XLM-R-Parla
nodes.summary: Introduces XLM-R-Parla (XLM-R-large DAPT on 1.72B words of 26-30 European parliaments incl. Italian) and the multilingual ParlaSent sentiment dataset; DAPT significantly improves downstream sentiment, rivaling GPT-4o zero-shot.
nodes.significance: Introduces XLM-R-Parla, the strongest peer-reviewed multilingual parliamentary DAPT encoder (XLM-R-large continued-pretrained on 1.72B words from 26+ European parliaments, including Italian register), together with the multilingual ParlaSent sentiment dataset. It is the flagship demonstration that parliamentary DAPT improves downstream political-text tasks, while the model has never been evaluated as an embedding or retrieval model.
nodes.findings: DAPT on 1.72B words of European parliamentary proceedings significantly improves downstream sentiment identification, including cross-lingual transfer, with fine-tuned models rivaling GPT-4o zero-shot performance.
nodes.limitations: The adaptation is MLM-only and evaluation is sentiment classification only; XLM-R-Parla has never been evaluated as an embedding or retrieval model and is not a usable sentence embedder out of the box.

nodes.label: Anisotropy of contextual embeddings
nodes.summary: All layers of BERT/ELMo/GPT-2 produce highly anisotropic representations confined to a narrow cone, worst in top layers.
nodes.significance: The foundational analysis showing that contextual embeddings from MLM-trained encoders are highly anisotropic, occupying a narrow cone in vector space. It is the root of the argument that MLM encoders, including domain-adapted ones, do not yield usable similarity spaces by mean-pooling alone.
nodes.findings: All layers of BERT, ELMo, and GPT-2 produce highly anisotropic representations confined to a narrow cone, with anisotropy worst in the top layers.
nodes.limitations: Later work (Fuster Baggetto & Fresno 2022) contests anisotropy as the root cause of poor sentence semantics, attributing both anisotropy and poor semantic isometry to frequency, subword, punctuation, and case biases.

nodes.label: SimCSE
nodes.summary: Unsupervised (dropout positives) and supervised (NLI) contrastive sentence embeddings; large STS gains; contrastive objective regularizes the anisotropic space.
nodes.significance: The minimal contrastive recipe for sentence embeddings, using dropout noise as unsupervised positives or NLI pairs as supervision. It shows that a contrastive objective regularizes the anisotropic MLM embedding space toward uniformity, making it the cheapest head to convert an MLM encoder into a sentence embedder.
nodes.findings: Unsupervised and supervised SimCSE with BERT-base reach 76.3 and 81.6 average Spearman on STS benchmarks respectively (+4.2 and +2.2 over prior best), and the contrastive objective demonstrably regularizes the anisotropic space.
nodes.limitations: Targets semantic textual similarity; STS gains do not guarantee retrieval gains, a point made explicitly by the TSDAE and GPL papers.

nodes.label: TSDAE
nodes.summary: Denoising-autoencoder sentence-embedding pretraining beats prior unsupervised methods and is explicitly shown to significantly outperform MLM as a domain-adaptation step for embeddings.
nodes.significance: A denoising-autoencoder objective for unsupervised sentence-embedding learning that is explicitly shown to significantly outperform MLM as a domain-adaptation step for embeddings. It is the direct published evidence that MLM is the wrong adaptation objective when the goal is retrieval-quality sentence vectors.
nodes.findings: TSDAE beats prior unsupervised sentence-embedding methods by up to 6.4 points on the USEB benchmark, reaches up to 93.1% of in-domain supervised performance, and significantly outperforms MLM as a pre-training/domain-adaptation step for sentence embeddings.

nodes.label: GPL (Generative Pseudo Labeling)
nodes.summary: Unsupervised domain adaptation of dense retrieval: synthetic queries + hard negatives + cross-encoder pseudo-labels + MarginMSE; up to +9.3 nDCG@10 on specialized BEIR domains, +1.4 more with TSDAE init.
nodes.significance: The reference method for unsupervised domain adaptation of dense retrievers: synthetic query generation, hard-negative mining, cross-encoder pseudo-labeling, and MarginMSE training on an unlabeled target corpus. It delivers the largest replicated label-free domain-adaptation gains for retrieval reported on specialized domains.
nodes.findings: On 6 domain-specialized BEIR datasets, GPL gains up to +9.3 nDCG@10 over an out-of-the-box state-of-the-art dense retriever, with TSDAE initialization adding a further +1.4 nDCG@10 on average; it is more robust than QGen and pseudo-labeling alternatives.
nodes.limitations: Published results are English-only; transfer to other languages requires a capable multilingual query generator and cross-encoder and remains undemonstrated.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: applying GPL to an Italian parliamentary corpus would be the first non-English and first parliamentary GPL result, since published numbers are English-only.

nodes.label: InPars
nodes.summary: GPT-3 few-shot prompting generates synthetic (query, doc) pairs; rerankers trained on them gain 7-30% over BM25.
nodes.significance: Showed that few-shot LLM prompting can generate synthetic (query, document) training pairs good enough to train effective neural rerankers without labeled data. Beyond training, the same generation step doubles as a bootstrap for building evaluation query sets in domains without existing relevance judgments.
nodes.findings: Neural rerankers trained on GPT-3-generated synthetic (query, document) pairs gain 7-30% over BM25 in nDCG/MRR.

nodes.label: Promptagator
nodes.summary: Few-shot dense retrieval from 8 examples: LLM as task-specific query generator with consistency filtering trains dual encoders beating ColBERTv2 on BEIR.
nodes.significance: Demonstrated few-shot dense retrieval: from as few as 8 annotated examples, an LLM used as a task-specific query generator with round-trip consistency filtering trains dual encoders that beat strong late-interaction baselines. Its key insight is that retrieval intents, not just domains, differ per task, so synthetic queries should mimic the target intent distribution.
nodes.findings: Task-specific dual encoders trained from 8 examples via LLM query generation and consistency filtering beat ColBERTv2 by more than 1.2 nDCG@10 on average across 11 BEIR datasets.

nodes.label: AdaSent
nodes.summary: A sentence-embedding adapter trained once on the base PLM can be inserted into any DAPT-ed variant, decoupling domain knowledge from sentence-embedding ability.
nodes.significance: The cleanest published articulation that domain knowledge (DAPT) and sentence-embedding ability (SEPT) are separable, composable ingredients: a sentence-embedding adapter trained once on the base PLM can be inserted into any domain-adapted variant. This decoupling is the conceptual frame for combining parliamentary or legal DAPT backbones with contrastive embedding heads.
nodes.findings: A sentence-embedding adapter trained once on the base PLM and inserted into DAPT-ed variants matches or surpasses full SEPT-on-DAPT training across 17 few-shot classification datasets at much lower cost.

nodes.label: ChipNeMo
nodes.summary: Industrial report: fine-tuning a small retriever with only 3,000 auto-generated domain samples improved retriever hit rate by ~30%, a better cost/benefit than full-model DAPT.
nodes.significance: An industrial datapoint showing that in a RAG system, adapting the retriever with a few thousand synthetic domain pairs yields larger, cheaper gains than full-model domain-adaptive pretraining. It sets the order of magnitude: thousands, not millions, of synthetic pairs suffice for large domain-retrieval improvements at moderate corpus scale.
nodes.findings: Fine-tuning e5_small_unsupervised with only 3,000 auto-generated domain samples improved retriever hit rate by ~30% over a pretrained state-of-the-art retriever, improving downstream RAG quality at a better cost/benefit than full-model DAPT.
nodes.limitations: Industrial technical report, not peer-reviewed; results are from the chip-design domain.

nodes.label: MMTEB
nodes.summary: Massive multilingual embedding benchmark (500+ tasks, incl. MTEB(Europe) with Italian): multilingual-e5-large-instruct (560M) is the best public model overall; no parliamentary/political retrieval task exists in any language.
nodes.significance: The massive community expansion of MTEB to 500+ tasks across 250-1000+ languages, including MTEB(Europe) with Italian retrieval tasks. It defines the strong open multilingual baseline any domain-adapted embedder must beat, while confirming that no parliamentary or political retrieval task exists in any embedding benchmark in any language.
nodes.findings: multilingual-e5-large-instruct (560M parameters) is the best-performing publicly available model on the multilingual aggregate, beating billion-scale LLM embedders; Italian retrieval coverage exists via MTEB(Europe) but is largely translation-derived.
nodes.limitations: Contains no parliamentary or political retrieval task in any language; Italian retrieval data is mostly translation-derived rather than native.

nodes.label: Wordscores
nodes.summary: Supervised text scaling: transfer word scores from reference texts with known (expert-survey) positions to virgin texts.
nodes.significance: The canonical supervised text-scaling method, establishing the field's core practice of validating text-derived political positions against expert surveys. It introduced the reference-anchor idea: transferring word scores from texts with known positions to place new texts on an externally anchored scale.
nodes.findings: Positions 'virgin' texts on an a-priori dimension by transferring word scores from reference texts with known expert-survey placements; estimated positions were validated via correlation with expert surveys and prior placements.
nodes.limitations: Strongly dependent on reference-text choice and reference scores, suffers vocabulary drift over time and score compression toward the middle, and performs poorly when virgin texts differ in genre from references.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: reference texts with known positions could anchor otherwise query-local ideological axes to an external scale.

nodes.label: Wordfish
nodes.summary: Unsupervised Poisson scaling of word frequencies onto one latent dimension; the recovered dimension is whatever dominates word-use variation, not necessarily left-right.
nodes.significance: The standard unsupervised text-scaling model (Poisson IRT on word counts) and the natural non-LLM baseline for any ideology-estimation pipeline. Its documented failure mode on parliamentary speech, recovering institutional rather than ideological dimensions, defines a key confound any speech-based positioning method must be tested against.
nodes.findings: Estimates a single latent dimension from relative word frequencies without reference texts, demonstrated on German party manifestos 1990-2005 and validated against expert judgments and CMP trends. The authors acknowledge the recovered dimension is whatever dominates word-use variation, not necessarily left-right.
nodes.limitations: On parliamentary floor speech the first latent dimension is often government-vs-opposition rather than ideology; results are sensitive to preprocessing and topic confounds, and validity is corpus-contingent (it replicated external benchmarks in Germany but failed in Denmark).

nodes.label: Wordshoal
nodes.summary: Two-stage legislative-speech scaling (per-debate Wordfish + cross-debate factor analysis); in the Irish Dail the dominant dimension is government vs opposition, not left-right.
nodes.significance: The first viable scaling of an entire legislature's speech corpus, decomposing estimation into per-debate scaling plus cross-debate factor analysis. It is the closest classic analogue to positioning on locally defined dimensions, and its central finding warns that speech-based positioning in high-discipline parliaments can recover institutional role rather than ideology.
nodes.findings: Scales each debate separately with Wordfish and extracts a common factor across debate-specific positions via Bayesian factor analysis. In the Irish Dail, the dominant dimension of parliamentary debate is government vs opposition, not left-right.
nodes.limitations: Locally estimated debate-level dimensions require an additional argument for cross-context comparability, and in high-discipline parliaments the recovered dimension reflects institutional role unless explicitly controlled.

nodes.label: Position taking in EP speeches
nodes.summary: Scaling European Parliament speeches recovers EU-integration and national divisions rather than left-right, even though left-right organizes EP voting.
nodes.significance: Key evidence that speech-derived party positions can systematically diverge from vote- or manifesto-derived positions, so imperfect correlation between speech-based estimates and expert surveys is partly substantive rather than pure error. Companion work also shows that access to the floor is strategically controlled, so who speaks is itself politically structured.
nodes.findings: Scaling European Parliament speeches recovers divisions over EU integration and national politics rather than left-right, even though left-right organizes EP roll-call voting.

nodes.label: Speeches vs votes (Swiss parliament)
nodes.summary: Speech-based ideal points correlate with vote-based ones but show greater intra-party spread; voting is discipline-constrained, speech less so.
nodes.significance: The standard empirical justification for speech-based ideological positioning: because voting is discipline-constrained while speech is less so, speech can reveal intra-party preference variation that roll calls hide. It also establishes cross-channel (speech vs vote) comparison as a convergent-validity design.
nodes.findings: Using the same Swiss MPs and bills with both votes and speeches, speech-based ideal points correlate with vote-based ones but show greater intra-party spread.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: speech-derived party positions could be cross-checked against large-scale roll-call vote data as a convergent-validity test across behavioral channels.

nodes.label: Scaling coded texts (Lowe et al.)
nodes.summary: Log odds-ratio scaling of manifesto category counts, validated against expert surveys; demonstrates construction of issue-specific scales beyond one left-right axis.
nodes.significance: The canonical demonstration that issue-specific party position scales can be constructed and validated separately from a single general left-right axis, providing the theoretical warrant for per-issue ideological measurement. It also warns that aggregate and issue-level scales can disagree, so issue-level estimates should be validated against matched-issue ground truth.
nodes.findings: Replaces RILE's additive pro-minus-con construction with a log odds-ratio scaling of manifesto category counts, validated against independent expert surveys, and explicitly builds multiple distinct policy dimensions beyond one left-right axis.
nodes.limitations: RILE-style aggregates and issue-specific scales can disagree, so results depend on which dimension is used as criterion.

nodes.label: Validating Wordscores
nodes.summary: Systematic validity framework for text scaling: content validity (which words drive scores), criterion validity (expert-survey correlation), construct validity (predicting known memberships).
nodes.significance: The most systematic validity framework applied to computational text scaling, articulating a three-part checklist: content validity (which words drive scores), criterion validity (correlation with expert surveys), and construct validity (predicting known group memberships). This checklist has become a template for validating any automated political-positioning method.
nodes.findings: Applying the three-part validity framework, Wordscores fails to deliver valid positions absent careful conditions.

nodes.label: Computers, coders, and voters
nodes.summary: Inter-method validation over 254 manifestos: Wordscores agrees with CMP/experts/voters in Germany and Denmark, Wordfish only in Germany; method validity is corpus-contingent.
nodes.significance: A large inter-method validation showing that the validity of automated position-estimation methods is corpus-contingent: a method that replicates external benchmarks in one country can fail in another. It motivates corpus-specific validation designs that triangulate automated estimates against expert, manifesto, and voter placements rather than assuming transfer from foreign successes.
nodes.findings: Across 254 manifestos and 33 elections in Germany and Denmark, Wordscores estimates agree with CMP, expert, and voter placements in both countries, while Wordfish agrees only in Germany.

nodes.label: Text as Data (validate, validate, validate)
nodes.summary: The field's governing doctrine: automated text measures have no default validity; every application must demonstrate the measure captures the claimed concept.
nodes.significance: The field's governing methodological doctrine for automated text analysis in political science: automated measures have no default validity, and every application must demonstrate that the measure captures the claimed concept ('validate, validate, validate'). Unsupervised outputs in particular require post-hoc interpretation plus external validation.

nodes.label: Human judgment as benchmark
nodes.summary: Validates text-scaling output against aggregated human judgments of the same texts when no external gold standard exists at the right granularity.
nodes.significance: Establishes aggregated human judgments of the same texts as a legitimate benchmark for validating text-scaling output when no external gold standard exists at the right granularity. This is the standard precedent for validating fine-grained (sentence- or fragment-level) stance estimates that no expert survey covers.
nodes.findings: Crowdsourced sentence-level judgments were aggregated and compared to text-scaling estimates, establishing human-judgment aggregation as a benchmark with quantified uncertainty.

nodes.label: Crowd-sourced text analysis
nodes.summary: Aggregated non-expert crowd codings of manifesto sentences reproduce expert codings; reproducibility as a validity criterion.
nodes.significance: Establishes that many redundant cheap judgments can substitute for few expert judgments in political text coding, and that reproducibility is itself a validity criterion. It legitimizes sentence- and fragment-level political judgments as a measurement unit and provides a design template for low-cost human validation arms.
nodes.findings: Aggregated non-expert crowd codings of manifesto sentences reproduce expert codings.

nodes.label: Party embeddings
nodes.summary: Doc2vec-style training with party-session indicator vectors over UK/Canada/US parliamentary corpora; principal components of party vectors recover validated left-right placements (validated against CMP, expert surveys, roll calls).
nodes.significance: The strongest published precedent that embedding-space geometry over parliamentary speech carries validated ideological signal, and the natural corpus-level baseline for any speech-based ideology pipeline. Its party-embedding construction underlies later parliamentary-benchmark alignment metrics.
nodes.findings: Augments doc2vec-style training with party-by-period indicator vectors over UK, Canadian, and US parliamentary corpora; principal components of the party vectors recover interpretable left-right placements validated against CMP indicators, expert surveys, and roll-call measures.

nodes.label: Cross-lingual embedding scaling
nodes.summary: Word-frequency scaling barely correlates with actual left-right placements while semantically-informed embedding scaling predicts positions better, with no cross-lingual drop.
nodes.significance: Early evidence that relative word usage is a poor proxy for ideology while semantically informed embedding-based scaling performs better, including across languages. It is a key citation for preferring semantic or LLM-based stance measurement over frequency-based projection, and for cross-lingual extension of position estimation.
nodes.findings: Word-frequency (Wordfish-style) scaling barely correlates with actual left-right placements, while semantically informed embedding scaling predicts party positions better, with no performance drop cross-lingually.

nodes.label: Linear political representations in LLMs
nodes.summary: Linear probes on LLM activations predict US lawmakers' DW-NOMINATE scores at Spearman ~0.8; steering along the probe direction shifts generated slant.
nodes.significance: Mechanistic-interpretability evidence that ideology exists as a linear direction in LLM representation space, providing indirect backing for axis-vector constructions of political position. It links internal model geometry to established external ideal-point measures.
nodes.findings: Linear probes on attention-head activations of Llama-2-7b-chat, Mistral-7b, and Vicuna predict US lawmakers' DW-NOMINATE scores at Spearman rho of about 0.8, with the representation concentrated in middle layers; steering along the probe direction shifts the slant of generated text.
nodes.limitations: The validated axis lives in the activation space of the probed model, not in an external text-embedding space, so the result does not directly license axis projection in generic embedding spaces.

nodes.label: LLM pairwise scaling of politicians
nodes.summary: LLM pairwise comparisons of senators aggregated with Bradley-Terry produce liberal-conservative and issue-specific scales correlating strongly with roll-call measures.
nodes.significance: Demonstrates that LLM pairwise comparisons aggregated with Bradley-Terry can produce both general and issue-specific political scales validated against external roll-call measures, suggesting LLMs synthesize diffuse public information rather than memorize scores. Pairwise elicitation is also a robustness alternative to direct scalar stance scoring.
nodes.findings: Prompting an LLM to compare senator pairs and scaling the comparison graph with Bradley-Terry yields liberal-conservative estimates that correlate strongly with DW-NOMINATE-type measures, and produces issue-specific scales (gun control, abortion) where roll-call data is sparse.
nodes.limitations: Preprint (working paper); no peer-reviewed publication found.

nodes.label: Measurement in the age of LLMs
nodes.summary: Elicits numeric ideology scores for legislators and texts directly from LLMs; scores accord with established scaling; frames LLMs as measurement instruments requiring criterion validation.
nodes.significance: Direct precedent for eliciting numeric ideology scores for legislators and texts from LLMs, framed within measurement theory: LLMs are treated as measurement instruments that require criterion validation against established scales.
nodes.findings: Numeric ideology scores elicited directly from an LLM accord closely with established scaling methods (DW-NOMINATE-style) and with the authors' judgment.
nodes.limitations: Preprint; no peer-reviewed venue found.

nodes.label: Positioning by asking and averaging
nodes.summary: Ask an LLM where a text stands on a focal dimension and average many responses: correlations with expert/crowd/roll-call benchmarks exceed .90 for best models, across 10 languages.
nodes.significance: The current benchmark paper for LLM-based political text positioning: asking an LLM where a text stands on a focal dimension and averaging many responses reaches expert-survey-grade agreement. It sets the achievable agreement ceiling for LLM positioning pipelines and gives 'averaging many small judgments' a citable pedigree, including multilingual validation.
nodes.findings: Averaging many GPT-4/Llama-3/Mixtral/Aya responses per actor or text yields correlations with expert, crowd, and roll-call benchmarks exceeding .90 for the best models, across US senators, UK manifestos, and EU policy speeches in 10 languages, zero-shot on European parties.

nodes.label: Mapping (A)Ideology (LLM vs CHES)
nodes.summary: GPT-3.5 pairwise party comparisons (names only, no text) aggregated with Bradley-Terry closely reproduce CHES orderings for European parties including Italy.
nodes.significance: European (Italy-inclusive) evidence that LLM-derived party orderings reproduce CHES expert-survey placements from party names alone, with no text input. This is both a validation of LLM political knowledge and the source of a crucial caveat: because the model already knows party reputations, corpus-free agreement with expert surveys is achievable, so evidence-grounded systems must show their outputs track the input text rather than the model's prior.
nodes.findings: GPT-3.5 pairwise 'which party is more right-wing' comparisons over all European party pairs (names and country only), aggregated with Bradley-Terry, closely reproduce CHES orderings, cross-validated against expert, manifesto, and poll-based estimates.
nodes.limitations: Because placements are produced from party names without any text, the design cannot separate model knowledge from evidence-based measurement; agreement reflects the LLM's prior about party reputations.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: an LLM-scored ideological compass must demonstrate it tracks retrieved parliamentary evidence rather than the model's prior about parties, e.g. via label-masking and label-shuffling tests.

nodes.label: ChatGPT vs expert survey (France)
nodes.summary: ChatGPT and local experts placed French parties on CHES items simultaneously: LLM close to experts on salient dimensions (left-right, EU, immigration), weaker on fringe issues and party characteristics.
nodes.significance: The exact template for per-issue validation of LLM party placement: an LLM and local experts completed the same CHES instrument simultaneously, revealing heterogeneous agreement across issue types. It grounds the pre-registered expectation that LLM agreement with expert surveys is highest on salient dimensions and lowest on fringe issues and party characteristics.
nodes.findings: ChatGPT placed French parties close to local experts on salient dimensions (left-right, EU integration, immigration) but was less accurate on fringe issues (free-market details, asylum specifics, urban-rural) and on party characteristics such as intra-party dissent and position blurring.
nodes.limitations: LLM placements are weakest exactly on dissent and position-blurring characteristics, which limits their use for estimating within-party heterogeneity.

nodes.label: LLM NLU-based scaling (AJPS)
nodes.authors: Benoit, De Marchi, Laver, Laver & Ma
nodes.summary: Argues for holistic 'read then score' LLM analysis of political texts against classify-and-count, benchmarked on crowd/expert data; the Wordscores authors migrating to LLM-NLU.
nodes.significance: Argues for holistic 'read then score' LLM analysis of political texts over sentence-level classify-and-count, benchmarked against crowd and expert data. That the original Wordscores authors are migrating to LLM-based natural language understanding is itself a signal of field consensus on the legitimacy of LLM scoring in political science.
nodes.findings: An LLM first summarizes a whole text's policy content and then scores it on issue scales; the holistic approach is compared favorably against classify-and-count using crowd and expert benchmarks.

nodes.label: Political Compass or Spinning Arrow?
nodes.summary: LLM political-compass results are unstable under paraphrase and format changes; constrained questionnaires do not reflect real usage.
nodes.significance: The central evaluation critique of 'political compass' style testing of LLMs: results are highly unstable under paraphrase and format changes, and constrained questionnaires do not reflect real usage. It effectively mandates prompt-perturbation robustness checks for any LLM-based political measurement pipeline.
nodes.findings: LLM political-compass results change substantially under paraphrase and answer-format changes (forced-choice vs open), and constrained questionnaire settings do not predict behavior in realistic usage.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: a compass that scores parliamentary evidence rather than the model's own opinions must still demonstrate paraphrase and format robustness empirically to answer this critique.

nodes.label: ChatGPT outperforms crowd workers
nodes.summary: Zero-shot ChatGPT beats MTurk crowds on relevance/stance/topic/frame annotation of political text with higher intercoder agreement.
nodes.significance: Baseline legitimacy result for LLM annotation of political text, showing zero-shot ChatGPT outperforming crowd workers on standard annotation tasks. Note that it measures agreement with researcher gold labels, not political neutrality of the annotations.
nodes.findings: Zero-shot ChatGPT beats MTurk crowds on relevance, stance, topic, and frame annotation over 6,183 tweets and articles, with roughly a 25-point accuracy advantage and higher intercoder agreement than trained annotators.
nodes.limitations: Measures agreement with researcher gold labels rather than political neutrality, so it cannot rule out politically asymmetric annotation error.

nodes.label: GPT-4 political annotation (Tornberg)
nodes.summary: GPT-4 beats experts and crowds at inferring party affiliation from tweets with equal or lower bias, introducing a party-asymmetric error metric.
nodes.significance: Shows GPT-4 outperforming both experts and crowd workers at political annotation while introducing a party-asymmetric error metric, i.e. measuring whether an annotator is systematically more accurate for one party than another. This asymmetry metric has become a standard bias diagnostic for LLM political annotation.
nodes.findings: GPT-4 infers party affiliation from tweets with higher accuracy and reliability than experts and crowd workers, and with equal or lower bias, where bias is measured as systematic asymmetry in error between parties.
nodes.limitations: Preprint; a peer-reviewed version was not confirmed.

nodes.label: LLMs as substitute annotators
nodes.summary: GPT-4 political text annotation approaches expert quality across tasks and languages; recommends keeping a human-coded validation subset.
nodes.significance: Shows that GPT-4 political text annotation approaches expert quality across several tasks and languages, while establishing the methodological norm of always keeping a human-coded validation subset and reporting agreement. It bounds how much trust to place in an LLM annotation layer.
nodes.findings: GPT-4 annotation of political text approaches expert quality across multiple tasks and languages.

nodes.label: Political bias in LLM stance classification
nodes.summary: 7 LLMs x 3 datasets: statistically significant stance-classification performance differences by political orientation of the target; telling the model about the bias does not fix it.
nodes.significance: Systematic evidence that LLM stance-classification accuracy differs by the political orientation of the target, and that simply informing the model of the bias does not fix it. This mandates per-party or per-orientation error analysis, rather than aggregate accuracy alone, for any LLM stance-scoring component.
nodes.findings: Across 7 LLMs, 3 datasets, and 4 prompting schemes, there are statistically significant stance-classification performance differences by the political orientation of the target; accuracy drops on ambiguous targets, and telling the model about the statement's political bias does not remove the effect.

nodes.label: Sentiment is not stance
nodes.summary: Sentiment classifiers systematically mismeasure stance (angry yet supportive speech); stance must be target-aware.
nodes.significance: Establishes the distinction between sentiment and stance in political text analysis: tone and position are separate constructs, and stance measurement must be target-aware. It is the standard citation for rejecting sentiment classifiers as stance measures and for requiring explicit handling of rebuttals and negative-tone support.
nodes.findings: Sentiment classifiers systematically mismeasure stance, for example on speech that is angry in tone yet supportive of the target position.

nodes.label: Preprocessing sensitivity
nodes.summary: Unsupervised text-analysis results, including scaling, can flip under defensible alternative preprocessing; sensitivity should be reported.
nodes.significance: Shows that unsupervised text-analysis results, including scaling, can flip under defensible alternative preprocessing choices, establishing the norm of reporting sensitivity across preprocessing regimes. The lesson generalizes to any pipeline whose upstream text-preparation choices (segmentation, clipping, batching, prompt wording) could alter downstream estimates.
nodes.findings: Unsupervised text-analysis results, including scaling estimates, can change qualitatively under defensible alternative preprocessing regimes; the paper recommends systematically reporting this sensitivity.

nodes.label: Evaluating expert judgments
nodes.summary: Psychometric toolkit for expert surveys: inter-expert reliability, expert-level bias, convergence with independent measures.
nodes.significance: The psychometric toolkit for expert surveys: inter-expert reliability via variance decomposition, expert-level bias, and validity via convergence with independent measures. It supplies the vocabulary for assessing the reliability of the criterion itself: disagreement with an expert survey on high-dissent items is uninformative and should be checked against the survey's own expert dispersion.

nodes.label: Cross-validating party positioning
nodes.summary: Compares expert survey vs manifesto vs voter survey vs elite survey on the same construct; expert surveys emerge as most accurate; founding paper of the triangulation doctrine.
nodes.significance: The founding paper of the triangulation doctrine in party positioning: no single gold standard exists, so expert surveys, manifestos, voter surveys, and elite surveys measuring the same construct should be cross-validated against each other. It is the direct methodological template for multi-source validation tables.
nodes.findings: Comparing expert survey, manifesto, voter survey, and elite survey measurements of party positioning on European integration, expert surveys emerge as the most accurate source.

nodes.label: GAL-TAN (Hooghe, Marks & Wilson)
nodes.summary: Origin of the GAL-TAN second dimension: economic left-right and cultural liberal-authoritarian are distinct, partially orthogonal axes.
nodes.significance: The origin of the GAL-TAN second dimension in European party politics: economic left-right and cultural liberal-authoritarian positioning are distinct, partially orthogonal axes. It provides the theoretical grounding for two-axis (economic plus cultural) representations of ideology rather than a single left-right scale.
nodes.findings: Economic left-right and GAL-TAN (green/alternative/libertarian vs traditional/authoritarian/nationalist) are shown to be distinct, partially orthogonal dimensions structuring European party positions.

nodes.label: Political preferences of LLMs
nodes.summary: 11 political-orientation instruments administered to 24 conversational LLMs: most RLHF'd chat models diagnosed left-of-center; modest fine-tuning steers orientation.
nodes.significance: Large-scale measurement of the political orientation of conversational LLMs, establishing the prior that RLHF-tuned generators carry a directional political lean independent of any retrieval corpus, so retrieval balance is necessary but not sufficient for output neutrality.
nodes.findings: Administering 11 political-orientation instruments to 24 conversational LLMs, most RLHF'd chat models are diagnosed left-of-center, base models are roughly incoherent/centrist, and modest supervised fine-tuning suffices to steer orientation.

nodes.label: Measuring ChatGPT political bias
nodes.summary: Impersonation-vs-default differencing with randomization and placebo tests finds systematic partisan lean (US, Brazil, UK).
nodes.significance: Introduces an impersonation-vs-default differencing design for measuring LLM political bias using within-model controls, randomization, dose-response, and placebo tests. The design transfers to auditing generated answers: a neutral answer should be roughly equidistant from persona-conditioned generations.
nodes.findings: Comparing ChatGPT's default answers to left/right-persona answers reveals systematic bias toward Democrats (US), Lula (Brazil), and Labour (UK), robust to randomization and placebo tests.

nodes.label: Whose opinions do LMs reflect? (OpinionQA)
nodes.authors: Santurkar, Durmus, Ladhak, Lee, Liang & Hashimoto
nodes.summary: Aligns LM answer distributions with Pew survey distributions for 60 US demographic groups; substantial misalignment; RLHF shifts models toward left-leaning demographics.
nodes.significance: Canonical method for distributional opinion alignment against external ground truth (OpinionQA): aligning LM answer distributions with survey distributions across demographic groups, with per-group representativeness reporting that transfers to per-party auditing.
nodes.findings: LM answer distributions show substantial misalignment with Pew survey distributions for 60 US demographic groups, with magnitude comparable to the Democrat–Republican gap on climate change; RLHF shifts models toward left-leaning, higher-educated demographics.

nodes.label: What is said and how it is said
nodes.summary: Decomposes political bias into content (stance substance) and style (framing/polarity); models can hold the same position while framing it asymmetrically.
nodes.significance: Decomposes political bias in LLMs into content (substance of the stance) and style (framing/lexical polarity), showing these can diverge. Directly relevant to answer auditing: equal quotation of groups with unequal framing is a failure mode that retrieval-side metrics cannot detect.
nodes.findings: Across policy issues on 11 open LLMs, models can hold the same substantive position while framing it asymmetrically, demonstrating that content balance and style balance are separate quantities.

nodes.label: Hidden Persuaders
nodes.summary: 18 LLMs show candidate preference in voting simulations; interaction with an LLM measurably shifted likely voters' views.
nodes.significance: Provides the stakes argument for political fairness in language systems: LLM political leaning is not just a measurement artifact but measurably shifts user opinions, justifying treating balance as a first-class evaluation objective in politically sensitive QA.
nodes.findings: 18 LLMs showed candidate preference (Biden over Trump) in voting simulations, and interaction with an LLM, even one not instructed to persuade, measurably shifted likely voters' views.

nodes.label: FA*IR fair top-k ranking
nodes.authors: Zehlike, Bonchi, Castillo, Hajian, Megahed & Baeza-Yates
nodes.summary: Ranked group fairness: every top-k prefix must contain a minimum fraction of protected-group items, tested against a binomial model; utility maximized subject to the constraint.
nodes.significance: Formalizes ranked group fairness as a prefix-representation constraint: every top-k prefix must contain a minimum fraction of protected-group items, tested against a binomial model, with utility maximized subject to the constraint. The formal ancestor of minimum-representation quotas in ranking.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: a fixed min-per-party quota is a prefix-representation constraint of this type, and the binomial-test machinery suggests statistically derived per-group floors instead of hard-coded ones.

nodes.label: Fairness of Exposure in Rankings
nodes.summary: Rank position allocates exposure; proposes optimizing rankings under exposure constraints, notably group exposure proportional to group merit (average relevance).
nodes.significance: Establishes that rank position allocates exposure and proposes optimizing rankings under exposure constraints, notably disparate exposure: group exposure proportional to group merit (average relevance). The literature precedent for conditioning fairness treatment on relevance rather than raw share, making exposure-proportional-to-merit the natural null hypothesis.

nodes.label: Equity of Attention
nodes.summary: Attention should be proportional to relevance amortized over a sequence of rankings, since a single ranking cannot be fair.
nodes.significance: Argues that attention should be proportional to relevance amortized over a sequence of rankings, since a single ranking cannot be fair. Justifies reporting fairness aggregated over query sets rather than per query, where balance can be structurally impossible.

nodes.label: Expected Exposure (Diaz et al.)
nodes.summary: Defines target exposure under an ideal randomizing policy and measures deviation, decomposable into disparity and relevance components.
nodes.significance: Defines expected exposure: target exposure under an ideal policy randomizing over equally relevant items, with deviation measured as expected exposure loss decomposable into disparity and relevance components. Gives a principled scalar separating 'unfairly treated' from 'just less relevant' for group-level exposure audits.

nodes.label: Fairness in Ranking survey
nodes.summary: Two-part ACM Computing Surveys taxonomy of fair-ranking formalizations and the normative assumptions each metric encodes.
nodes.significance: Two-part ACM Computing Surveys taxonomy of fair-ranking formalizations (pre-, in-, and post-processing; probability-based vs exposure-based group fairness; individual fairness) and of the normative assumptions each metric encodes. The standard citation for classifying fairness mechanisms and stating the normative worldview a system adopts.

nodes.label: Should I Follow the Crowd?
nodes.summary: Probabilistic separation of item popularity from true relevance; popularity-rewarding offline metrics can invert true effectiveness.
nodes.significance: Cleanest conceptual precedent for 'observed frequency is not relevance': a probabilistic model separating item popularity from true relevance, showing popularity-rewarding offline metrics can invert true effectiveness. Motivates counterfactual reweighting designs that evaluate treatment under equalized observation.
nodes.findings: The probabilistic analysis identifies conditions where following popularity is safe versus misleading and proves that popularity-rewarding offline metrics can invert true effectiveness, validated with a crowdsourced dataset free of exposure bias.

nodes.label: Popularity bias survey
nodes.summary: Catalogues popularity-bias metrics (popularity lift, Gini over exposure, recommendation-vs-popularity correlation) and mitigation families, plus feedback-loop amplification evidence.
nodes.significance: Survey of popularity bias in recommender systems, cataloguing detection metrics (popularity lift, Gini over exposure, recommendation-vs-popularity correlation) and mitigation families (regularization, causal/IPS debiasing, post-hoc calibration), plus feedback-loop amplification evidence. Establishes output-share-on-input-popularity regression as standard practice.

nodes.label: Controlling popularity bias in LtR
nodes.summary: Adds a popularity-dispersion regularizer to learning-to-rank to balance head vs tail item exposure.
nodes.significance: Introduces regularization-based control of popularity bias in learning-to-rank: a popularity-dispersion regularizer balancing head versus tail item exposure. Shows that in-processing penalties on over-represented groups are an established debiasing pattern.

nodes.label: Does RAG introduce unfairness?
nodes.summary: Scenario-based fairness evaluation of RAG: fairness issues persist in both retrieval and generation stages even when utility improves; multi-stage architectures make mitigation hard.
nodes.significance: Scenario-based fairness evaluation of RAG systems showing that fairness must be audited stage by stage: multi-stage architectures make mitigation hard because components optimize different objectives, and each stage carries a distinct bias mechanism.
nodes.findings: Fairness issues persist in both the retrieval and generation stages of RAG even when utility improves.

nodes.label: No Free Lunch (RAG undermines fairness)
nodes.authors: Hu, Wu, Guan, Zhu, Guo, Qi & Li
nodes.summary: RAG can undo fairness alignment without fine-tuning; even fully censored external corpora still yield biased outputs: the retrieval mechanism itself introduces bias.
nodes.significance: Adversarial analysis showing retrieval augmentation can undo fairness alignment in LLMs without any fine-tuning; even fully censored, 'unbiased' external corpora still yield biased outputs because the retrieval mechanism itself introduces bias. The sharpest counter to arguments that neutral corpus provenance guarantees neutral outputs.
nodes.findings: Under a three-level threat model ordered by user vigilance, RAG undermines fairness alignment without fine-tuning, and biased outputs persist even when the external corpus is fully censored.
nodes.limitations: arXiv-only preprint at the time of review, not peer-reviewed.

nodes.label: Towards FairRAG (exposure at retrieval time)
nodes.summary: On TREC Fair Ranking data, representative stochastic rankers achieve near-parity exposure, and generation demographic parity closely mirrors exposure parity.
nodes.significance: Empirical support for enforcing group balance at retrieval time rather than in the generation prompt: exposure-fair stochastic rankers propagate their parity into generation-side demographic parity.
nodes.findings: On TREC 2022 Fair Ranking data, a Representative Stochastic ranker achieves near-parity average exposure, and generation demographic parity closely mirrors exposure parity, indicating retrieval is the effective intervention point.
nodes.limitations: Single-author arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed; results should be treated as supporting rather than load-bearing.

nodes.label: When Not to Trust Language Models (PopQA)
nodes.authors: Mallen, Asai, Zhong, Das, Khashabi & Hajishirzi
nodes.summary: LM factual recall tracks entity popularity; retrieval augmentation helps precisely on unpopular entities.
nodes.significance: Establishes that LM factual recall tracks entity popularity (PopQA) and that retrieval augmentation helps precisely on unpopular entities, motivating adaptive retrieval. Implies generator parametric priors about political entities are popularity-skewed even when retrieval is balanced.
nodes.findings: LM factual recall correlates with entity popularity measured by Wikipedia pageviews; retrieval augmentation yields its gains mainly on unpopular entities, supporting popularity-adaptive retrieval.

nodes.label: What Drives Media Slant?
nodes.summary: Text-based slant index: outlet language similarity to congressional partisan phrase distributions, then regression-decomposed onto demand and supply factors.
nodes.significance: Foundational text-based slant index: outlet language similarity to partisan phrase distributions from the legislative record, with slant then regression-decomposed onto candidate causes. Supplies both a method for measuring the partisan slant of generated text against per-party speech distributions and the regression-decomposition template for calibration analyses.
nodes.findings: Newspaper slant measured against congressional partisan phrase frequencies is driven substantially by demand-side factors: reader ideology explains roughly 20% of slant variation, with little role for owner identity.

nodes.label: Fair and Balanced? (crowdsourced media bias)
nodes.summary: 749 judges classify 10,950 articles: bias manifests mostly as issue selection and lopsided negative coverage of the out-group, not overt advocacy.
nodes.significance: Large-scale crowdsourced measurement of media bias showing that bias manifests mostly as issue selection and lopsided negative coverage of the out-group rather than overt advocacy. Warns that fairness is not only how much each group appears but in what light, motivating valence-lopsidedness statistics per group.
nodes.findings: 749 judges classified 10,950 articles (sampled from 803k) across 15 US outlets; outlets were more similar than commonly assumed, and detected bias took the form of topic selection and disproportionately negative out-group coverage.

nodes.label: Pretraining term frequencies
nodes.summary: Few-shot accuracy strongly correlates with pretraining term frequency (up to ~70-point gaps between frequency deciles).
nodes.significance: Demonstrates that LLM few-shot performance is strongly tied to pretraining term frequency, revealing that apparent capability partly reflects frequency memorization. The general mechanism predicting quality disparities for infrequent entities and groups at generation time.
nodes.findings: Few-shot accuracy correlates strongly with pretraining term frequency, with up to ~70-point absolute accuracy gaps between top and bottom frequency deciles.

nodes.label: Long-tail knowledge (Kandpal et al.)
nodes.summary: QA accuracy scales with the count of relevant pretraining documents; retrieval augmentation is the effective long-tail mitigation.
nodes.significance: Shows QA accuracy scales with the number of relevant pretraining documents and that retrieval augmentation is the effective mitigation for long-tail knowledge. Together with related frequency studies, establishes the corpus-frequency triad: frequency drives model behavior, and retrieval fixes the tail.
nodes.findings: QA accuracy scales with the count of relevant pretraining documents; retrieval augmentation substantially mitigates the performance gap on long-tail knowledge.

nodes.label: Perspective-varied political summarization
nodes.summary: Benchmark for independently summarizing each political perspective in opinionated documents; all 11 tested models struggle to stay faithful to the intended perspective.
nodes.significance: Benchmark for perspective-varied political summarization: independently summarizing each political perspective in opinionated documents. Provides evidence that perspective-conditioned summarization is hard for current models and supplies evaluation dimensions for perspective faithfulness.
nodes.findings: All 11 benchmarked models struggle to stay faithful to the intended perspective when summarizing opinionated political documents, with GPT-4o performing relatively best.

nodes.label: MODS (moderated multi-perspective summarization)
nodes.authors: Balepur, Siu, Lipka, Dernoncourt, Sun, Boyd-Graber & Mathur
nodes.summary: Panel architecture of per-document speaker LLMs plus a moderator with a topic plan: 38-59% gains in topic coverage and perspective balance, with citation-based balance metrics.
nodes.significance: Panel-discussion architecture for balanced multi-perspective summarization of debatable queries: per-document speaker LLMs plus a moderator LLM with a topic plan, evaluated with citation-based balance metrics. The closest architectural precedent for per-group expert selection with staged, balance-aware generation.
nodes.findings: On ConflictingQA and DebateQFS, the moderated mixture-of-speakers design yields 38–59% gains in topic coverage and perspective balance over baselines, measured with citation-based balance metrics.

nodes.label: ParlaMint 5.0
nodes.summary: 29 uniformly TEI-encoded European parliamentary corpora (8.07M speeches, 1.23B words, >20 languages, mostly 2015-2022) with speaker/party/role metadata, a mandatory chair/regular/guest speaker taxonomy, and v5.0 CAP topic labels; CC BY 4.0 on CLARIN.SI.
nodes.significance: The field's reference collection: 29 uniformly TEI-encoded European parliamentary corpora (8.07M speeches, 1.23B words, >20 languages, mostly 2015-2022) with speaker/party/role metadata, a mandatory chair/regular/guest speaker taxonomy, and CAP topic labels added in v5.0. Its encoding conventions are the de-facto European standard for parliamentary corpus construction.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: a graph data model over parliamentary records should align with the ParlaMint TEI schema, whose speaker-type taxonomy is the citable standard for procedural filtering.

nodes.label: ParlaMint-IT (Senato)
nodes.summary: Italian ParlaMint component: Senato della Repubblica only, ~2013 to ~mid-2022 (legislatures XVII-XVIII), ~79k speeches, ~31M words, TEI + UD annotation.
nodes.significance: The Italian component of ParlaMint, covering the Senato della Repubblica from ~2013 to ~mid-2022 (legislatures XVII-XVIII) with ~79k speeches and ~31M words in TEI with Universal Dependencies annotation. It is the principal machine-actionable Italian parliamentary corpus within the European comparable-corpus ecosystem.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: different chamber and essentially disjoint time window from Camera XIX, so usable for cross-chamber transfer and distributional checks rather than as gold overlap.

nodes.label: ItaParlCorpus
nodes.summary: Italian Camera dei Deputati speeches 1948-2022 (legislatures I-XVIII): ~2.4M speeches, 470M words, 5,830 speakers, 77 parties, CC BY 4.0 on Harvard Dataverse.
nodes.significance: The main historical corpus of the Italian Camera dei Deputati: ~2.4M speeches and 470M words spanning 1948-2022 (legislatures I-XVIII), with 5,830 speakers and 77 parties, released CC BY 4.0. It enables diachronic analysis and large-scale training on Italian parliamentary language.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: coverage ends in 2022 exactly where a Camera XIX corpus begins, making it a natural domain-adaptive pretraining corpus for an Italian parliamentary encoder and a historical validation substrate.

nodes.label: Knesset Corpus
nodes.summary: All Israeli plenary and committee protocols of ~3 decades: >30M sentences, >384M tokens, morpho-syntactic and NER annotation, speaker metadata; CC BY 4.0.
