nodes.summary: Proposes Corrective Retrieval-Augmented Generation (CRAG), which adds a lightweight retrieval evaluator to assess the quality of retrieved documents and trigger corrective actions. Depending on a confidence judgment it keeps, discards, or supplements retrieved passages with web search, and decomposes-then-recomposes documents to filter irrelevant content.
nodes.significance: A method for making RAG robust to poor retrieval by evaluating and correcting retrieved evidence before generation.
nodes.limitations: Relies on a retrieval evaluator whose confidence thresholds and optional web-search fallback add components that must be tuned and trusted.

nodes.label: RAG with Source Reliability
nodes.summary: Proposes a reliability-aware RAG framework that estimates the reliability of each source and incorporates these estimates into generation so that more trustworthy sources are weighted more heavily. It extends standard RAG to settings where retrieved documents vary in credibility.
nodes.significance: Addresses source credibility in RAG by explicitly modeling and propagating per-source reliability into the generation step.
nodes.limitations: Accurate reliability estimation may require supervision or assumptions about source quality that are not always available.

nodes.label: RAG Domain Adaptation (end-to-end)
nodes.authors: Siriwardhana, Weerasekera, Wen, Kaluarachchi, Rana & Nanayakkara
nodes.summary: Studies domain adaptation of RAG for open-domain QA by jointly training the retriever and generator end-to-end, including updating the document encoder so the external knowledge index adapts to the target domain. It evaluates the approach on specialized domains such as healthcare, news, and conversations.
nodes.significance: Shows that end-to-end training of both retriever and generator improves RAG transfer to specialized domains compared with adapting the generator alone.
nodes.limitations: Jointly updating the document encoder requires periodic re-encoding of the knowledge index, increasing training cost.

nodes.label: SQuAD
nodes.summary: Reading comprehension benchmark of 100,000+ crowdsourced question-answer pairs on 500+ Wikipedia articles, where each answer is a contiguous span of the associated passage; answering requires extracting the span rather than generating free text.
nodes.significance: The benchmark that anchored the extractive machine reading comprehension paradigm and became a standard reference point for span-based question answering, shaping how later QA datasets were constructed and evaluated with exact-match and token-level F1 metrics.
nodes.findings: Contains 107,785 question-answer pairs over 536 Wikipedia articles; a strong logistic-regression baseline reached 51.0% F1 while human performance was 86.8% F1 at release.
nodes.limitations: Answers are restricted to spans present in a single supplied passage, so the task does not cover open-domain retrieval, multi-hop reasoning, or unanswerable questions (addressed only in the later SQuAD 2.0 release).

nodes.label: Natural Questions
nodes.authors: Kwiatkowski, Palomaki, Redfield, Collins, Parikh, Alberti, Epstein, Polosukhin, Devlin, Lee, Toutanova, Jones, Kelcey, Chang, Dai, Uszkoreit, Le & Petrov
nodes.summary: Question answering benchmark built from real anonymized Google search queries, each paired with a full Wikipedia page and annotated with a long answer (a passage) and, when present, a short answer span; it supports both retrieval and reading evaluation.
nodes.significance: A large benchmark that moved QA evaluation toward naturally occurring information-seeking queries over full documents rather than questions written against a known passage, making it a common testbed for open-domain retrieval-then-read systems.
nodes.findings: Comprises 307,373 training examples with single annotations plus 7,830 development and 7,842 test examples with 5-way annotations; human upper bounds were reported at 87% F1 for long answers and 76% F1 for short answers.
nodes.limitations: Annotation is grounded in Wikipedia only and many queries have no short answer, and the long/short answer annotation scheme requires careful handling, complicating direct comparison with span-only benchmarks.

nodes.label: HotpotQA
nodes.authors: Yang, Qi, Zhang, Bengio, Cohen, Salakhutdinov & Manning
nodes.summary: Multi-hop question answering dataset of 113,000 Wikipedia-based questions that require reasoning over two or more supporting documents, with sentence-level supporting-fact annotations that enable explainability evaluation alongside answer accuracy.
nodes.significance: Established multi-hop reasoning with explicit supporting-fact supervision as a distinct QA evaluation setting, influencing later work on retrieval over multiple passages and on grounding answers in identifiable evidence sentences.
nodes.findings: Contains about 113,000 question-answer pairs; the paper reports that requiring multiple supporting documents and providing sentence-level supporting facts yields questions not answerable from a single passage.
nodes.limitations: Questions are synthetically composed from entity bridges and comparisons over Wikipedia, so reasoning patterns can be exploitable by shortcuts and may not reflect naturally occurring multi-hop information needs.

nodes.label: Faithfulness & Factuality in Summarization
nodes.summary: Large human study of abstractive summarization systems measuring hallucination, annotating whether generated content is faithful to the source and whether it is factual, and comparing these judgments against standard automatic metrics.
nodes.significance: A foundational empirical demonstration that neural abstractive summarizers hallucinate content pervasively and that faithfulness is distinct from factuality, while showing that ROUGE and similar overlap metrics correlate poorly with human faithfulness judgments; textual-entailment signals correlated best.
nodes.findings: Human annotation of summaries showed that the large majority of model-generated summaries contained hallucinated content, and that over 70% of single-sentence summaries from the studied systems had hallucinations; standard metrics like ROUGE correlated weakly with faithfulness.
nodes.limitations: The study centers on the XSum English news dataset and a fixed set of neural summarizers, so hallucination rates and metric correlations may not transfer to other domains or to retrieval-grounded generation.

nodes.label: Hallucinated but Factual!
nodes.summary: Inspects hallucinations in abstractive summarization and distinguishes hallucinations that are factual with respect to world knowledge from those that are non-factual, introducing annotation and detection to separate the two categories rather than treating all unsupported content as error.
nodes.significance: Refines the hallucination framing by showing that content not entailed by the source is not uniformly erroneous, separating factual hallucinations from non-factual ones and motivating evaluation that treats source-ungrounded but true statements differently from fabrications.
nodes.findings: Annotation of entity-level hallucinations found that a substantial share of hallucinated entities were in fact factual rather than erroneous, indicating that source-entailment alone overcounts factual errors.
nodes.limitations: Relies on news-domain summarization data and on external world-knowledge judgments that are themselves hard to adjudicate, and the factual/non-factual distinction depends on knowledge resources that may be incomplete.

nodes.label: Survey of Hallucination in NLG
nodes.authors: Ji, Lee, Frieske, Yu, Su, Xu, Ishii, Bang, Madotto & Fung
nodes.summary: Comprehensive survey of hallucination across natural language generation tasks, organizing definitions, the intrinsic vs extrinsic distinction, contributing causes, and mitigation and evaluation methods spanning summarization, dialogue, generative QA, data-to-text, and machine translation.
nodes.significance: A widely cited reference that consolidated hallucination terminology and taxonomy across generation tasks before the large-language-model era, providing the shared vocabulary (intrinsic vs extrinsic, faithfulness vs factuality) that later hallucination surveys and detection methods build upon.
nodes.limitations: Predates the large-scale instruction-tuned LLM and retrieval-augmented generation literature, so its coverage of LLM-specific hallucination causes and mitigations is limited relative to later surveys.

nodes.label: Bias in NLP: A Critical Survey
nodes.summary: Critical survey of 146 papers on bias in NLP, arguing that the literature is conceptually fragmented and often fails to state what is meant by bias, why it is harmful, and to whom.
nodes.significance: A widely cited survey that establishes a framework for motivating and operationalizing bias research in NLP, distinguishing harms (allocational vs. representational) and urging that normative claims about bias be made explicit and grounded in the lived experience of affected communities.
nodes.findings: Surveyed 146 papers on bias in NLP; found that the majority provide vague, inconsistent, or unstated motivations for what constitutes bias and rarely engage with relevant social-science literature.
nodes.limitations: Offers conceptual guidance and a taxonomy rather than concrete measurement methods or benchmarks; scope is limited to work published up to 2020.

nodes.label: Tracking Political Biases in NLP Models
nodes.summary: Traces political bias from pretraining corpora through language models to downstream tasks, probing LMs on a political-compass instrument and measuring how the resulting leaning propagates into hate-speech and misinformation classifiers.
nodes.significance: Connects three stages of the NLP pipeline by showing that the political leaning of pretraining data is inherited by language models and then shapes the fairness of downstream classifiers, providing a methodology for auditing ideological bias end to end.
nodes.findings: Positioned a range of LMs on a two-axis political-compass map, finding measurable social and economic leanings that differ by model; classifiers fine-tuned on these LMs showed uneven performance across target groups depending on the LM's political leaning.
nodes.limitations: Relies on a political-compass test as the ideology instrument, which is a coarse and contestable measure; focuses on English models and a limited set of downstream tasks.

nodes.label: Bias on the Web
nodes.summary: Review of the many forms of bias that arise on the Web and in the systems built on it, distinguishing activity, data, sampling, algorithmic, and interaction biases and the feedback loops that amplify them.
nodes.significance: An influential overview that frames bias as a pervasive, self-reinforcing property of Web data and the algorithms that mine it, giving a vocabulary for how ranking and retrieval systems can encode and amplify pre-existing inequities.
nodes.limitations: A conceptual review rather than an empirical study; it catalogs bias types and feedback loops without proposing concrete mitigation techniques or measurements.

nodes.label: Discovering Diverse Perspectives about Claims
nodes.summary: Introduces the task of discovering diverse perspectives about a claim together with supporting evidence, and presents the PerspectRUM dataset of claims, perspectives, and evidence paragraphs.
nodes.significance: Frames perspective discovery as a structured retrieval-and-stance problem, establishing a task and dataset for surfacing the range of substantiated stances on a debatable claim rather than a single answer.
nodes.findings: Released PerspectRUM, a dataset of around 1,000 claims with multiple perspectives and supporting evidence paragraphs; baseline systems fell well short of human performance on retrieving and clustering diverse perspectives.
nodes.limitations: The dataset covers English debate-style claims and relies on crowd judgments of stance and relevance, which may not transfer to specialized domains such as legislative discourse.

nodes.label: PerSphere
nodes.authors: Li, Li, Qi, Guo, Guo, Zhang & Zhang
nodes.summary: Proposes PerSphere, a framework and benchmark for multi-faceted perspective retrieval and summarization that retrieves evidence for opposing viewpoints on a query and produces a structured, balanced summary of the contrasting perspectives.
nodes.significance: Combines perspective-aware retrieval with summarization so that outputs represent multiple sides of a contested topic, offering a benchmark for evaluating whether systems surface balanced rather than one-sided answers.
nodes.limitations: A preprint without peer review at time of indexing; evaluation centers on the framework's own benchmark, so generalization to other domains and languages is not established.

nodes.label: Perspectives in Play
nodes.summary: Presents a multi-perspective approach for building more inclusive NLP systems, modeling disagreement and diverse annotator viewpoints rather than collapsing labels to a single majority judgment.
nodes.significance: Argues that retaining and modeling multiple perspectives improves inclusiveness and fairness of NLP systems, contributing methods and evaluation for handling annotator disagreement as signal rather than noise.
nodes.limitations: Evaluation is bounded to the tasks and datasets studied in the paper; the benefit of perspective modeling may depend on the availability of richly annotated disagreement data.

nodes.label: Using LMs to Simulate Human Samples
nodes.authors: Argyle, Busby, Fulda, Gubler, Rytting & Wingate
nodes.summary: Proposes conditioning large language models on demographic and attitudinal backstories drawn from survey respondents so that generated text reproduces the response distributions of the corresponding human subpopulations, a procedure the authors term 'silicon sampling'.
nodes.significance: Articulates the 'algorithmic fidelity' criterion and popularizes using demographically conditioned LLM outputs as proxies for human samples, framing a line of work on whether model-generated opinions track the underlying human populations.
nodes.limitations: Fidelity is demonstrated for specific US survey contexts and model versions; conditioning captures correlational patterns in training data rather than causally grounded individual attitudes, and coverage varies across subgroups.

nodes.label: Measuring Group Differences in Congressional Speech
nodes.summary: Develops a multinomial-choice model with a penalized estimator for measuring how partisan groups differ in their high-dimensional discrete choices, correcting the finite-sample bias that inflates naive estimates of group differences, and applies it to phrase usage in US Congressional speech.
nodes.significance: Provides an econometric framework and bias-corrected estimator for quantifying partisan differences in language from high-dimensional text, separating genuine polarization signal from sampling-induced overstatement.
nodes.findings: Bias-corrected estimates show partisan differences in US Congressional speech were roughly flat until the early 1990s and then rose sharply, far lower than uncorrected maximum-likelihood estimates imply.
nodes.limitations: Focuses on US Congressional phrase frequencies under a specific model of discrete choice; results depend on phrase-construction and penalization choices and are descriptive rather than causal.

nodes.label: Stance Detection: A Survey
nodes.summary: Surveys stance detection research, defining the task of automatically determining the position (favor, against, neither) expressed in text toward a target, and reviewing datasets, features, approaches, and related tasks such as sentiment analysis and argument mining.
nodes.significance: A reference overview that consolidates task definitions, benchmark datasets, and methods for stance detection, and clarifies its boundaries with adjacent tasks like sentiment classification.
nodes.limitations: A survey current to 2020, predating much transformer-based stance work; it organizes the literature rather than providing new empirical results.

nodes.label: SemEval-2016 Task 6: Stance in Tweets
nodes.summary: A shared-task benchmark of English tweets annotated for stance (favor, against, none) toward five predefined targets plus an unlabeled-target track, distinguishing stance from tweet sentiment, with a supervised subtask and a weakly supervised subtask.
nodes.significance: An early and widely reused benchmark that operationalized target-specific stance detection on social media and established the favor/against/none labeling scheme used by much subsequent work.
nodes.findings: Covers five targets with about 4,870 annotated tweets; the best supervised systems reported macro-F1 in the low-to-mid 0.7 range, with stance and sentiment shown to be related but distinct labels.
nodes.limitations: Limited to English tweets on a small fixed set of targets, so coverage and domain transfer to longer or non-social-media text are constrained.

nodes.label: IPSA Corpus
nodes.summary: Italian Parliament corpus covering both chambers (Senato and Camera), including speeches, committee reports, and law proposals across roughly 175 years (1848-present), with historical material OCR-digitised.
nodes.significance: A large-span resource for the Italian Parliament that unifies material from both chambers and several document genres (plenary speeches, committee reports, law proposals) over about 175 years, with older volumes recovered through OCR. It broadens the available Italian parliamentary material beyond single-chamber or single-genre collections and supports diachronic and cross-chamber analysis.
nodes.limitations: Italian only; historical portions rely on OCR, which can introduce transcription noise in older material.

nodes.label: Talk of Norway
nodes.summary: A richly annotated corpus of speeches from the Norwegian Parliament (Storting) covering 1998-2016, with metadata on speakers, parties, and roles alongside linguistic annotation.
nodes.significance: A well-documented national parliamentary corpus for Norwegian that pairs the full text of Storting debates with speaker, party, and role metadata plus linguistic annotation, enabling both political-science and NLP analyses of legislative discourse.
nodes.limitations: Norwegian only; coverage ends in 2016.

nodes.label: Europarl
nodes.summary: A parallel corpus extracted from European Parliament proceedings covering 11 languages, originally built to support statistical machine translation.
nodes.significance: A foundational and heavily reused parliamentary resource: aligned European Parliament proceedings in 11 languages that became a standard benchmark for statistical machine translation and multilingual NLP more broadly.
nodes.limitations: Built primarily for machine translation, so it provides limited structured speaker or procedural metadata compared with later purpose-built parliamentary corpora.

nodes.label: EP Debates as Linked Open Data
nodes.authors: Van Aggelen, Hollink, Kemman, Kleppe & Beunders
nodes.summary: An RDF/Linked Open Data representation of European Parliament debates, modelling speeches, speakers, and proceedings as interlinked structured data.
nodes.significance: Demonstrates modelling parliamentary proceedings as Linked Open Data, turning European Parliament debates into an interlinked RDF resource that connects speeches, speakers, and sessions and enables semantic querying over legislative records.
nodes.limitations: Focused on the European Parliament; the value of the representation depends on the completeness and quality of the underlying source proceedings.

nodes.label: Multilingual Power and Ideology Identification
nodes.authors: Çöltekin, Kopp, Meden, Morkevicius, Ljubešić & Erjavec
nodes.summary: A ParlaMint-derived reference dataset for multilingual political orientation (left-right) and power (government vs. opposition) identification, with simple baseline classifiers.
nodes.significance: Provides a multilingual reference dataset and baselines for two parliamentary classification tasks, orientation (left-right) and power (governing vs. opposition), derived from ParlaMint across many national parliaments, establishing a shared setup for comparable cross-lingual evaluation.
nodes.limitations: Labels are derived from party-level metadata, so they approximate rather than directly measure the stance of individual speeches; baselines are intentionally simple.

nodes.label: QA-GNN
nodes.summary: A method that jointly reasons over a language model and a knowledge graph for question answering by building a working graph from the QA context and scoring/pruning KG nodes via relevance to the question.
nodes.significance: An influential approach to grounding question answering in structured knowledge: it couples a language model with a retrieved knowledge-graph subgraph and uses graph neural reasoning with question-conditioned relevance scoring, offering an alternative to purely text-based or LLM-only QA.
nodes.limitations: Relies on the availability and quality of a relevant KG subgraph; evaluated on commonsense and science QA rather than institutional or parliamentary settings.

nodes.label: Unifying LLMs and KGs: A Roadmap
nodes.authors: Pan, Luo, Wang, Chen, Wang & Wu
nodes.summary: A roadmap surveying how large language models and knowledge graphs can be combined, organised around KG-enhanced LLMs, LLM-augmented KGs, and synergized LLM+KG frameworks.
nodes.significance: A widely cited synthesis of the intersection between large language models and knowledge graphs, offering a structured taxonomy of ways the two can reinforce each other and a reference framing for building knowledge-grounded LLM systems.
nodes.limitations: A survey rather than an empirical study; it frames directions and categories but does not itself benchmark the approaches it catalogues.

nodes.label: A Survey on Knowledge Graphs
nodes.summary: A comprehensive survey of knowledge graphs covering representation learning, knowledge acquisition (extraction and completion), and downstream applications.
nodes.significance: A broad reference survey of the knowledge-graph field, organising work on KG representation learning, acquisition via information extraction and completion, and application areas, serving as an entry point to the methods underlying KG construction and use.
nodes.limitations: A survey rather than a new system; predates the most recent LLM-era developments in KG construction.

nodes.label: Latent Dirichlet Allocation
nodes.summary: Introduces a generative probabilistic topic model in which each document is a mixture over latent topics and each topic a distribution over words, inferred via variational methods.
nodes.significance: LDA established the dominant unsupervised topic modeling framework, providing a probabilistic basis for discovering latent thematic structure in large text collections and underpinning many later extensions that condition topics on metadata such as authors or time.
nodes.limitations: Requires the number of topics to be fixed in advance, assumes bag-of-words exchangeability, and produces topics that may need human interpretation.

nodes.label: SummEval
nodes.authors: Fabbri, Kryscinski, McCann, Xiong, Socher & Radev
nodes.summary: Re-evaluates summarization evaluation by collecting consistent human judgments and re-scoring a broad set of automatic metrics and model outputs on CNN/DailyMail.
nodes.significance: Provides a reproducible meta-evaluation resource showing weak and inconsistent correlations between many widely used automatic summarization metrics and human judgments, informing how summarization quality should be measured.
nodes.limitations: Centered on a single English news summarization dataset, limiting generalization to other domains, languages, or abstractive settings.

nodes.label: Testing Statistical Significance in NLP
nodes.summary: Surveys statistical significance testing for NLP, offering guidance on selecting appropriate tests for comparing model performance and a decision procedure for common experimental settings.
nodes.significance: Offers practical, widely cited guidance on choosing and applying significance tests in NLP experiments, raising the standard for statistically sound comparison of systems.
nodes.limitations: Focuses on single-metric comparisons and does not fully cover multiple-comparison correction or effect-size and equivalence testing.

nodes.label: Inter-Coder Agreement for CL
nodes.summary: Reviews and formalizes chance-corrected agreement coefficients for annotation in computational linguistics, clarifying the assumptions behind kappa, alpha, and related measures.
nodes.significance: Serves as the standard methodological reference for measuring and reporting inter-annotator agreement in computational linguistics, grounding the choice of coefficients in explicit assumptions.
nodes.limitations: Primarily theoretical guidance; does not prescribe domain-specific thresholds for acceptable agreement.

nodes.label: All That's Human Is Not Gold
nodes.authors: Clark, August, Serrano, Haduong, Gururangan & Smith
nodes.summary: Studies how reliably untrained human evaluators can distinguish machine-generated from human-written text and how evaluation protocol choices affect judgments.
nodes.significance: Demonstrates that human evaluation of generated text is itself fragile and protocol-dependent, motivating more careful design and reporting of human studies for text generation.
nodes.limitations: Examines English text and a limited set of generation tasks and evaluator populations.

nodes.label: Argument Mining: A Survey
nodes.summary: Surveys the field of argument mining, organizing tasks such as argument component identification, relation extraction, and argument structure detection along with methods and resources.
nodes.significance: Provides a consolidated map of argument mining tasks, techniques, and datasets, serving as a reference point for research on extracting argumentative structure from text including political discourse.
nodes.limitations: As a survey it predates later large-language-model approaches and does not report new empirical results.

nodes.label: Learning to Rank Academic Experts (DBLP)
nodes.summary: Applies learning-to-rank methods that fuse multiple sources of evidence, including textual and graph-based features, to rank candidate experts in the DBLP academic dataset.
nodes.significance: Shows that supervised learning-to-rank combining heterogeneous evidence can improve expert retrieval over single-signal baselines, contributing to expertise-retrieval methodology.
nodes.limitations: Evaluated on a single academic domain (DBLP), and effectiveness depends on the availability of labeled training data and engineered features.

nodes.label: ParlLawSpeech parliamentary text collection
nodes.authors: Christian Rauh, Lukas Hetzer, Sven-Oliver Proksch, Jan Schwalbach, Miklós Sebők
nodes.summary: A collection of more than three million bills, laws and parliamentary speeches from Austria, Czechia, Croatia, Denmark, Germany, Hungary, Spain and the European Parliament. Documents of the same legislative procedure share a procedure identifier, so speeches link to the bills they debate and the laws that result. Released through GESIS (DOI 10.7802/2824).
nodes.significance: The largest cross-national resource that links parliamentary speech to legislative output. Italy is not covered.
nodes.findings: Contributions: harmonised multi-country bill, law and speech corpora with procedure-level linkage. The linkage design is a template for connecting debate to legislative outcomes.
nodes.limitations: Italy and the Italian Chamber are not included (from the dataset description).

nodes.label: TRACE: accountable agentic retrieval for archives
nodes.authors: Donghan Bian, Marie Puren, Florian Cafiero
nodes.summary: A training-free agentic retrieval system with source traceability, built for French Third Republic parliamentary debates and press in the DECIDON project. Evaluated on the HistoriQA benchmark against sparse, dense, graph and agentic RAG baselines.
nodes.significance: The first retrieval system reporting effectiveness numbers on a parliamentary QA benchmark, with accountability of sources as a design goal.
nodes.findings: On HistoriQA: R@10 0.856 and MRR 0.653, ahead of sparse, dense, graph-based and agentic RAG baselines.
nodes.limitations: Historical corpus (Third Republic); evaluation on a single benchmark (from the abstract).

nodes.label: Political text scaling comparability: 17 algorithms
nodes.summary: Builds shared infrastructure to run 17 political text-scaling algorithms under comparable conditions, with 5,537 runs producing about 4.25 million left-right estimates, and measures how sensitive each algorithm is to its hyperparameters.
nodes.significance: A large-scale sensitivity analysis of text-scaling methods: it locates where configuration choices actually change ideological estimates.
nodes.findings: For 13 of 17 algorithms hyperparameters explain little variance (ICC < .10). Where sensitivity exists it comes from the choice of embedding model, seed keyword lists and the number of topics.
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: Blame attribution in the Danish Parliament
nodes.authors: Markus Lundsfryd Jensen, Rune Egeskov Trust, Kenneth Christian Enevoldsen, et al.
nodes.summary: Trains BlameBERT (F1 0.80) to detect political contrasting and blame attribution, and applies it to Folketing debates from 1997 to 2026.
nodes.significance: Large-scale evidence on how government and opposition differ in adversarial rhetoric in a European parliament.
nodes.findings: Opposition parties blame far more than government parties; ideology moderates the effect.
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: Linking Bundestag speakers to Wikidata
nodes.authors: Thomas Haider, Arne Cypionka, Maximilian Teich
nodes.summary: Links every speaker of the German Bundestag from 1949 to 2021 to Wikidata and audits the scope and coverage of the resulting biographical metadata.
nodes.significance: A route to external biographical signals for parliamentary speakers, together with an audit of how unevenly such metadata is covered.
nodes.findings: Coverage of attributes such as gender and profession is uneven across speakers, which can bias any downstream use.
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: Issue bias in AI writing assistance: Swedish 2026 election
nodes.authors: Bastiaan Bruinsma, Annika Fredén, Paul Röttger, et al.
nodes.summary: Collects 148k responses from six LLMs to 107 policy propositions in a writing-assistance setting and compares them with the positions of Sweden's eight parliamentary parties.
nodes.significance: A party-level, non-US measurement of political issue bias in LLM writing assistance.
nodes.findings: The Social Democrats sit closest to every model, but no within-model difference between parties survives multiple-comparison correction.
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: Retrieval sensitivity to identity signals in queries
nodes.authors: Andrew Tang, Nicholas Deas, Kathleen McKeown, et al.
nodes.summary: Tests whether retrievers change what they return when a query carries political identity signals, across five dense retrievers and BM25, and probes query embeddings for political lean.
nodes.significance: Shows that political bias enters at the retrieval stage, before any generation.
nodes.findings: All five dense retrievers and BM25 return articles matching the political lean signalled in the query. Linear probes recover that lean from query embeddings beyond token-level features.
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: Ideological mimicry in LLMs (Poli-SHIFT)
nodes.authors: Olivia Macmillan-Scott, Michael Jacobs, Nils Metternich, et al.
nodes.summary: Introduces the Poli-SHIFT dataset to measure how user terminology and premises shift the political stance an LLM expresses.
nodes.significance: Quantifies framing sensitivity: the wording of a political question can flip the side a model supports.
nodes.findings: Changing terminology alone reverses the supported side in 16.9% of matched comparisons.
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: ItColBERT: Italian late-interaction retriever
nodes.summary: Trains the first Italian-specialised ColBERT retriever (135M parameters) and reports what helped and what did not.
nodes.significance: A language-specific late-interaction baseline for Italian retrieval.
nodes.findings: Inference-time chunking gave +0.06 nDCG@10 and beat further training; pre-registered hard-negative mining failed to help.
nodes.limitations: General-domain Italian; no parliamentary evaluation.

nodes.label: Family-conditioned preference in LLM-as-judge panels
nodes.authors: David Ababio Awuni, Luke E. K. Achenie, Benjamin Tei Partey, et al.
nodes.summary: Measures, over 9,312 crossed judgments, whether LLM judges prefer outputs from models of their own family, using a corrected estimator, and how panel composition changes outcomes.
nodes.significance: Direct evidence that judge panel composition is itself a source of bias in LLM-based evaluation.
nodes.findings: A 3.4-8.4 percentage-point same-family lift for every family; 55% of AB/BA pairs reverse; panel composition changes 18.5% of outcomes.
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: GAUGE: when not to trust LLM judges in user-simulated evaluation
nodes.authors: Umesh Bodhwani, Thanh Tran, Kai Wei
nodes.summary: Audits the LLM user-simulator and LLM-judge gates used to evaluate task-oriented agents against verifiable rewards, and proposes calibrating the judge against those rewards.
nodes.significance: An audit of judge reliability against ground truth, with a calibration recipe.
nodes.findings: Judges rate agents from their own model family higher; "satisfied" ratings miss 57.5% of failed tasks; close comparisons are picked wrong 31% of the time (as reported in the NLP Newsletter summary; unverified against the full text).
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: Statistics over LLM judges (evalstats)
nodes.summary: Shows that standard tests run on raw LLM-judge scores inflate false positives and adds prediction-powered corrections for rank tests (Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney), with guidance for small-sample evaluation.
nodes.significance: Practical calibrated inference for evaluations that rely on LLM judges and few human labels.
nodes.findings: Raw-score testing inflates false positives; PPI-corrected rank tests restore calibrated error rates.
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: Synthetic vs authentic query distributions in RAG evaluation
nodes.authors: Filip J. Kucia, Barbara M. Gawlik
nodes.summary: Compares synthetic and authentic query distributions in RAG evaluation and tests whether system choices tuned on synthetic queries carry over to real ones.
nodes.significance: Shows that synthetic test queries can lead to the wrong retrieval configuration.
nodes.findings: Synthetic queries average 15.7 words, real ones 6.8. Tuning on synthetic queries selected a hybrid retriever, because BM25 helped only long queries.
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: The attribution-compression frontier in RAG
nodes.summary: Measures how context compression before generation affects citation attribution, checking citations both against compressed summaries and against original source spans.
nodes.significance: Shows a trade-off between compressing retrieved context and keeping citations attributable to the source text.
nodes.findings: Abstractive compression keeps citations that look precise against summaries (0.86) but not against source spans (0.12).
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: EvidenT: evidence groundedness and traceability
nodes.authors: Anubha Kabra, Katie Jooyoung Kim, Colin Zhiwei Kou, et al.
nodes.summary: An enterprise assistant that deterministically aligns extracted evidence to retrieved text before generation, so every cited span exists in the sources.
nodes.significance: A deployed verbatim-span grounding system; it has no entailment check on top of the lexical alignment.
nodes.findings: No citations to non-retrieved URLs; +29% gold-source hits.
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: CITECHOICE: presentation and citation credit
nodes.summary: A causal audit of how the way documents are presented to an agentic search system redistributes which sources get cited.
nodes.significance: Shows that citation exposure depends on presentation and rank, not only on relevance.
nodes.findings: Structured rendering concentrates citation credit (+0.50 citations per answer); citation gap between rank 1 and rank 5 is 42 points.
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: AstaBrief 8B: cited scientific report generation
nodes.summary: An open-weights 8B model (built on Qwen3-8B) that writes a fully cited scientific report from a question and retrieved literature excerpts in a single pass. Trained with SFT on 47K examples and DPO on 6K preference pairs from real Asta queries; weights and data on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0.
nodes.significance: An open baseline for citation-grounded long-form generation from retrieved documents.
nodes.findings: About 3.5x faster than the frontier-model mode it replaces (51 s vs 178 s per report). A simple data-filtering heuristic mattered more for citation quality than the training algorithm.
nodes.limitations: Not peer-reviewed; scientific-literature domain.

nodes.label: Parliamentary debates in The World Avatar: hybrid RAG
nodes.authors: Sebastian Mosbach, Jiawei Lai, Kushagar Rustagi, Dan N. Tran
nodes.summary: A hybrid RAG system for questions about German Bundestag debates that combines retrieval over speech text with retrieval over structured metadata in a knowledge graph, embedded in The World Avatar dynamic knowledge graph.
nodes.significance: A parliamentary RAG system that mixes text and knowledge-graph retrieval to answer relational questions about parties and debates.
nodes.findings: Answers questions beyond keyword search, such as which parties most often supported one another or when topics drew strong audience reactions.
nodes.limitations: Preprint; no quantitative evaluation reported in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: Transcribing Italian parliamentary speeches with VLMs
nodes.authors: Luigi Curini, Alfio Ferrara, Giovanni Pagano, et al.
nodes.summary: Uses vision-language models to transcribe and recognise speeches from scanned Italian parliamentary records.
nodes.significance: A digitisation route for historical Italian parliamentary records that are only available as scans.
nodes.findings: Shows VLMs can transcribe and segment Italian parliamentary speech records (details not verified beyond the abstract).
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: Mitigating bias in RAG by controlling the embedder
nodes.authors: Taeyoun Kim, Jacob Springer, Aditi Raghunathan, Maarten Sap
nodes.summary: Studies how bias in RAG output, including political bias, depends on the embedder, and whether adjusting the embedder can offset bias coming from the generator.
nodes.significance: Places the embedder, not only the LLM, at the centre of bias control in RAG.
nodes.findings: RAG output bias tracks embedder bias; tuning the embedder can counteract generator bias (from the abstract).
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: Political neutrality as balanced approval (PARETO)
nodes.authors: Jonathan Stray, David Zhai Yang, Steven Luo, et al.
nodes.summary: Defines political neutrality of AI responses as balanced approval across the political spectrum and measures it with a large-scale human evaluation.
nodes.significance: An operational, human-grounded definition of a politically balanced answer.
nodes.findings: Large-scale human ratings make it possible to compare responses by how evenly they are approved across political groups (details not verified beyond the abstract).
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.label: ACL-Verbatim: hallucination-free QA for research
nodes.authors: Gábor Recski, Szilveszter Tóth, Nadia Verdha, et al.
nodes.summary: An extractive question-answering system over research papers that answers only with verbatim spans from the sources.
nodes.significance: An extractive alternative to generative citation: answers are quoted, not paraphrased.
nodes.findings: Verbatim extraction removes hallucinated content by construction (details not verified beyond the abstract).
nodes.limitations: Specific limitations not enumerated in the abstract (unverified).

nodes.findings: Model cards report accuracy 0.967 for the binary German BERT model, 0.93 for the XLM-R variant, 0.83 on German tweets, and weighted F1 0.59 for the five-class sentiment model.
nodes.limitations: Preprint; figures come from the Hugging Face model cards (the OSF page was unavailable on 2026-10-17). Binary results are reported as accuracy on a class-imbalanced task, with no per-class F1, and the cards disagree on the base model of the English-named checkpoint.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: the codebook and the binary task transfer directly to Italian speeches, where an EU-salience signal per group and per year could be computed over the whole XIX legislature.
nodes.label: Detecting EU sentiment in texts (Lattmann)
nodes.summary: Fine-tunes BERT-family classifiers on about 1,700 hand-annotated Bundestag sentences to detect EU speech (explicit or implicit references to the EU) and to grade EU sentiment in five classes: EU speech, more integration, policy scepticism, EU praise, hard Euroscepticism.
nodes.significance: The released models make EU salience measurable at sentence level, a prerequisite for Euroscepticism research on parliamentary text at scale.

nodes.findings: Without expert-annotated data GPT performed best (F1 0.74); with a curated dataset few-shot classification reached F1 0.87.
nodes.limitations: Details beyond the abstract not verified.
nodes.label: Identifying Euroscepticism with text-as-data
nodes.summary: Compares supervised classification, transfer learning, GPT and few-shot classification for Euroscepticism in parliamentary speeches, against crowdsourced and expert annotation.
nodes.significance: One of the few peer-reviewed comparisons of LLM and few-shot approaches for Euroscepticism on parliamentary speech.

nodes.venue: ECPR Standing Group on Central and East European Politics conference, Cluj 2026
nodes.limitations: Conference paper; results known only from the abstract.
nodes.label: EU politicization in Slovak parliamentary speeches
nodes.summary: Uses proprietary and open LLMs to classify EU stance and sentiment in about 30,000 speeches of the Slovak National Council (1994-2023), validated on more than 600 expert-coded speeches with custom EU-stance guidelines.
nodes.significance: Treats EU stance and EU sentiment as separate targets and tests whether cheaper open models can replace proprietary ones at corpus scale.

nodes.authors: Marone, Weller, Fleshman, Yang, Lawrie & Van Durme
nodes.limitations: Not yet compared with parliamentary DAPT encoders such as XLM-R-Parla.
nodes.label: mmBERT: a modern multilingual encoder
nodes.summary: ModernBERT-based encoder trained on more than 3T tokens in over 1,800 languages (base: 307M parameters), with inverse mask scheduling and late inclusion of low-resource languages.
nodes.significance: Claims the first clear improvement over XLM-R as a massively multilingual encoder for classification, embedding and retrieval, and is already the backbone of the European Parliament's EuroVoc classifier.

nodes.limitations: Single parliament and small training set; metrics reported as accuracy only for the binary models.
nodes.label: EU-speech sentence classifiers (Lattmann)
nodes.summary: Binary sentence classifiers (German BERT, English BERT, XLM-R base) that flag explicit or implicit references to the EU, plus a five-class EU-sentiment model, all trained on about 1,700 Bundestag sentences.
nodes.significance: Ready-to-use baselines for EU-reference detection; the XLM-R variant can be applied zero-shot to other languages.

nodes.limitations: No Italian training data; MIT-licensed model card without an accompanying paper.
nodes.label: EUroBerta-xlm (EU reference detector)
nodes.summary: XLM-R base fine-tuned on 5,950 ParlSpeech sentences from seven parliaments (AT, DK, DE, NL, ES, SE, UK; 1999-2019) to classify EU vs no-EU references; reported F1 0.944.
nodes.significance: The broadest multilingual EU-reference classifier found; a second annotation round targeted false positives (geographic Europe, sports such as UEFA) and oversampled radical-right parties.

nodes.limitations: No benchmark results published; trained on legislative and institutional prose, not on parliamentary speech.
nodes.label: EUBERT (European Parliament)
nodes.summary: Uncased BERT (about 100M parameters) pretrained on 30 years of EU Publications Office documents in 24 languages, released under EUPL-1.2.
nodes.significance: A domain encoder for EU institutional language that includes Italian; a candidate backbone for classifiers of EU-related content.

nodes.limitations: Trained on EU legal documents; accuracy on parliamentary speech is unmeasured.
nodes.application: Potential relevance to a system like ParliamentRAG: a EuroVoc subject layer for Italian acts and speeches that is comparable across EU parliaments.
nodes.label: EuroVoc multi-label classifier (European Parliament)
nodes.summary: mmBERT-base fine-tuned on about 327,000 CELLAR documents to assign EuroVoc concepts (21 domains, 127 micro-thesauri, 7,062 concepts) in 24 languages; domain-level F1 0.733.
nodes.significance: An off-the-shelf multilingual subject tagger aligned with the EU's official thesaurus, presented by its authors as a tagging assistant whose proposals a person confirms.

nodes.label: EuroVoc thesaurus
nodes.summary: The EU's multilingual, multidisciplinary thesaurus used to index EU documents, organised in domains, micro-thesauri and concepts, published as linked data.
nodes.significance: The shared subject vocabulary behind EUBERT and the EuroVoc classifier, and a natural bridge between national parliamentary records and EU legislation.

nodes.label: EU reference and Euroscepticism detection
nodes.summary: Detecting whether a sentence or speech refers to the European Union, explicitly or implicitly, and grading its stance toward European integration.
nodes.significance: Measures EU salience and Euroscepticism in national parliaments; stance and sentiment must be kept apart.

nodes.label: No validated EU-reference classifier for Italian parliamentary speech
nodes.summary: Published EU-reference classifiers are trained on German, Slovak or ParlSpeech parliaments; none found (search of 2026-10-17) trained or evaluated on Italian parliamentary speech.
nodes.significance: Without Italian gold data, cross-lingual transfer of the existing models cannot be measured.

nodes.label: How salient is the EU in the Italian Parliament, by group and over time?
nodes.summary: Build an Italian codebook and gold set, pre-label with an LLM, fine-tune an encoder student and compare it with zero-shot transfer of the existing EU-speech models over Camera and Senate XIX speeches.
nodes.significance: Would yield the first Italian EU-reference resource and a per-group EU-salience measure that respects party components.
nodes.short: How salient is the EU in th…

nodes.venue: mySociety method page and blog posts
nodes.limitations: The method page does not explain how direction is set.
nodes.label: TheyWorkForYou voting summaries (mySociety)
nodes.summary: Manual method that assigns each UK vote to a policy as aligned or against and separates votes that count from informative ones. Posts of 13/3/2025 and 8/7/2025 discuss reasoned amendments: assent at second reading does not indicate agreement.
nodes.significance: Part of the political-science literature on what a recorded vote means when agenda power and strategic voting are at play.

nodes.findings: Successful killers with identifiable strategic voting are "extremely rare".
nodes.limitations: Details beyond the abstract not verified.
nodes.label: "Killer" Amendments in Congress
nodes.summary: Examines 76 alleged killer amendments in the 103rd and 104th Congress.
nodes.significance: Part of the political-science literature on what a recorded vote means when agenda power and strategic voting are at play.

nodes.findings: Five cases.
nodes.limitations: Details beyond the abstract not verified.
nodes.label: In Search of Killer Amendments in the Modern U.S. House
nodes.summary: Searches House roll calls 1953-2004 for killer amendments, with a necessary condition: the bill is amended, then defeated.
nodes.significance: Part of the political-science literature on what a recorded vote means when agenda power and strategic voting are at play.

nodes.limitations: Details beyond the abstract not verified.
nodes.label: The Paradox of Voting and Congressional Rules for Voting on Amendments
nodes.summary: Founding text on amendment voting rules.
nodes.significance: Part of the political-science literature on what a recorded vote means when agenda power and strategic voting are at play.

nodes.limitations: Student venue; review unverified.
nodes.label: Killer Amendments and Strategic Voting in the Senate
nodes.summary: Studies killer amendments and strategic voting in the 109th Congress.
nodes.significance: Part of the political-science literature on what a recorded vote means when agenda power and strategic voting are at play.

nodes.limitations: Text read through an automatic extract.
nodes.label: Representation, Competing Principals, and Waffling on Bills in US Legislatures
nodes.summary: Studies legislators who sponsor a bill and vote against it at final passage, across 46 state lower houses and the US House. Explains the behaviour by cross-pressure and does not reconstruct position.
nodes.significance: Part of the political-science literature on what a recorded vote means when agenda power and strategic voting are at play.

nodes.limitations: Details beyond the abstract not verified.
nodes.label: Limited Obstruction
nodes.summary: Formal model of who can delay legislation without holding a veto.
nodes.significance: Part of the political-science literature on what a recorded vote means when agenda power and strategic voting are at play.

nodes.findings: Governing coalitions are almost never rolled on final votes, against about 20% for opposition parties.
nodes.limitations: Details beyond the abstract not verified.
nodes.label: Agenda Power in the Italian Chamber of Deputies, 1988-2000
nodes.summary: Measures how often parties are rolled on final votes in the Italian Chamber.
nodes.significance: Part of the political-science literature on what a recorded vote means when agenda power and strategic voting are at play.

nodes.limitations: Details beyond the abstract not verified.

edges.evidence: Maynez et al. argue faithfulness and factuality must be measured separately from ROUGE-style overlap, anticipating fine-grained factuality evaluation.

edges.explanation: Cao et al. build on the faithfulness/factuality distinction by further partitioning hallucinations into factual and non-factual categories.
edges.evidence: The paper inspects hallucinations and shows a substantial fraction are factual with respect to world knowledge rather than errors.

edges.explanation: Distinguishing factual from non-factual hallucinations sharpens the separation between source-faithfulness and world-correctness.
edges.evidence: Annotated hallucinated entities are split into factual and non-factual, directly operationalizing the correctness-vs-faithfulness gap.

edges.explanation: Because some hallucinations are factual, source-entailment detectors such as SummaC flag true-but-ungrounded content as inconsistent, which Cao et al.'s distinction exposes.
edges.evidence: The paper shows a large share of source-unentailed entities are nonetheless factual, which pure entailment-based inconsistency detectors would misclassify.

edges.explanation: Both examine factual consistency of summaries, but Cao et al. reframe unsupported content as potentially factual rather than uniformly scoring it as inconsistent.
edges.evidence: QAFactEval scores factual consistency against the source, whereas Cao et al. demonstrate that source-ungrounded content can still be factual.

edges.explanation: Both are surveys of hallucination, but Ji et al. cover classical NLG tasks before the LLM era while the later survey centers on large language models.
edges.evidence: Ji et al. organize hallucination across summarization, dialogue, and data-to-text generation, predating the instruction-tuned LLM literature emphasized in the 2025 survey.

edges.explanation: The survey draws on empirical hallucination studies in summarization, including the faithfulness/factuality findings, to build its taxonomy.
edges.evidence: Ji et al. consolidate the intrinsic/extrinsic and faithfulness/factuality distinctions established by summarization hallucination studies.

edges.explanation: The survey catalogs entailment-based factual-consistency detection as a mitigation and evaluation strategy exemplified by SummaC.
edges.evidence: Ji et al. review NLI-based consistency metrics among the faithfulness evaluation methods surveyed.

edges.explanation: The survey formalizes intrinsic vs extrinsic hallucination and faithfulness vs factuality, providing the vocabulary for the correctness-vs-faithfulness concept.
edges.evidence: Ji et al. define and distinguish faithfulness to the source from factual correctness across generation tasks.

edges.explanation: Both are surveys that organize a research area; Blodgett surveys bias conceptualizations across NLP broadly while Abercrombie & Batista-Navarro survey sentiment and position-taking in parliamentary text.
edges.evidence: Blodgett et al. 2020 abstract (critical survey of 146 bias-in-NLP papers); Abercrombie & Batista-Navarro 2020 parliamentary survey.

edges.explanation: Blodgett's insistence that bias claims name the harm, the mechanism, and the affected group motivates treating systematic disadvantage toward smaller parties as a concrete allocational-harm concept.
edges.evidence: Blodgett et al. 2020 taxonomy of allocational vs. representational harms and call to specify who is harmed.

edges.explanation: Blodgett's argument that analyses must make normative and measurement choices explicit supports Card et al.'s practice of defining and filtering procedural speech before computing substantive measures.
edges.evidence: Blodgett et al. 2020 on explicit operationalization; Card et al. 2022 procedural-speech classification methodology.

edges.explanation: Both empirically locate LLMs on a political-ideology instrument; Feng et al. trace leaning back to pretraining data and forward to downstream tasks, while Rozado measures political preferences across many conversational LLMs.
edges.evidence: Feng et al. 2023 political-compass probing of LMs; Rozado 2024 'Political preferences of LLMs'.

edges.explanation: Both quantify the political/opinion leaning of language models; Santurkar et al. measure whose opinions LMs reflect via OpinionQA, whereas Feng et al. attribute leaning to pretraining corpora and track downstream effects.
edges.evidence: Feng et al. 2023 two-axis LM leaning map; Santurkar et al. 2023 OpinionQA study.

edges.explanation: Feng et al. extend the idea, formalized by Gentzkow & Shapiro for media, that the slant of a text source is driven by the data it is built from, applying it to pretraining corpora of language models.
edges.evidence: Gentzkow & Shapiro 2010 media slant; Feng et al. 2023 pretraining-data-to-model leaning analysis.

edges.explanation: By showing that model leaning produces uneven downstream treatment of different groups, Feng et al. speak to systematic bias against particular political actors such as smaller parties.
edges.evidence: Feng et al. 2023 finding that LM leaning yields disparate downstream classifier fairness across target groups.

edges.explanation: Baeza-Yates's account of feedback loops that amplify Web bias underpins the popularity-bias phenomena Klimashevskaia et al. survey in recommendation and retrieval.
edges.evidence: Baeza-Yates 2018 on activity/data bias and amplification; Klimashevskaia et al. 2024 popularity-bias survey.

edges.explanation: The review's discussion of how activity and sampling bias cause popular items to dominate is a direct conceptual source for popularity bias as a retrieval concept.
edges.evidence: Baeza-Yates 2018 analysis of interaction and activity bias favoring already-popular content.

edges.explanation: Both are surveys of bias in information systems; Baeza-Yates frames bias across the Web broadly, while Zehlike et al. focus on fairness in ranking and mitigation methods.
edges.evidence: Baeza-Yates 2018 'Bias on the Web'; Zehlike et al. 2022 fairness-in-ranking survey.

edges.explanation: Baeza-Yates's framing of data and sampling bias supports Budak et al.'s empirical effort to measure slant in media content rather than assume neutrality of the sources.
edges.evidence: Baeza-Yates 2018 on data bias; Budak et al. 2016 crowdsourced measurement of media bias.

edges.explanation: The task of surfacing multiple substantiated perspectives on a claim anticipates MODS's moderated multi-perspective summarization covering contrasting viewpoints.
edges.evidence: Chen et al. 2019 diverse-perspective discovery task; MODS 2025 moderated multi-perspective summarization.

edges.explanation: Framing evidence-grounded diverse perspectives on debatable claims anticipates Deas & McKeown's perspective-varied political summarization dataset and task.
edges.evidence: Chen et al. 2019 PerspectRUM task; Deas & McKeown 2025 perspective-varied political summarization.

edges.evidence: Chen et al. 2019 perspective+evidence retrieval; PerSphere 2024 multi-faceted perspective retrieval and summarization.

edges.explanation: Explicitly discovering the full range of stances on a claim is a mechanism against silencing minority viewpoints, speaking to under-representation of smaller actors.
edges.evidence: Chen et al. 2019 goal of surfacing diverse rather than dominant perspectives on a claim.

edges.explanation: PerSphere extends the perspective-discovery-with-evidence task into a combined multi-faceted retrieval and summarization framework with a dedicated benchmark.

edges.explanation: Both produce balanced multi-perspective summaries over contested topics; PerSphere couples perspective retrieval with summarization while MODS emphasizes moderation of competing viewpoints.
edges.evidence: PerSphere 2024 balanced perspective summarization; MODS 2025 moderated multi-perspective summarization.

edges.explanation: PerSphere's contribution is a method and benchmark for producing perspective-balanced summaries, directly serving the summarization task.
PerSphere retrieves evidence for each opposing viewpoint before summarizing, making perspective-aware retrieval a core component.

edges.evidence: PerSphere 2024 design for balanced coverage of opposing perspectives.

edges.explanation: Perspectives in Play operationalizes the inclusiveness and harm-to-whom concerns raised by Blodgett et al. by modeling diverse annotator viewpoints instead of a single majority label.
edges.evidence: Blodgett et al. 2020 call to center affected communities; Muscato et al. 2025 multi-perspective inclusive NLP approach.

edges.explanation: Both treat multiple perspectives as signal; Perspectives in Play models annotator disagreement for inclusiveness, while Deas & McKeown build perspective-varied political summarization resources.
edges.evidence: Muscato et al. 2025 multi-perspective disagreement modeling; Deas & McKeown 2025 perspective-varied political summarization.

edges.explanation: Retaining minority annotator perspectives instead of collapsing to the majority is a direct countermeasure to marginalizing smaller or minority viewpoints.
edges.evidence: Muscato et al. 2025 argument for preserving multiple perspectives rather than majority-only labels.

edges.explanation: Its multi-perspective evaluation lens motivates disaggregating system quality by viewpoint, relevant to assessing whether output quality is even across parties.
edges.evidence: Muscato et al. 2025 evaluation framing around per-perspective system behavior.

edges.explanation: Both probe whether LLM-generated opinions align with human survey populations; Argyle argues for fidelity via demographic conditioning while Santurkar measures representativeness gaps.

edges.explanation: Both assess whether language models reproduce the political positions of human groups, offering complementary evidence on LLMs as proxies for human attitudes.
edges.evidence: Argyle conditions models on respondent backstories to recover opinion distributions; Wu et al. (2023) estimate LLMs' political positions relative to human reference points.

edges.explanation: Argyle's evidence that conditioned LLM outputs track human response patterns supports the broader case for using LLMs in place of human annotators/respondents.
edges.evidence: Gilardi et al. (2023) report LLMs outperforming crowd workers on text-annotation tasks, consistent with Argyle's fidelity claim for simulated human samples.

edges.explanation: Both measure partisan language differences in US political text, but the 2019 paper introduces a bias-corrected high-dimensional estimator addressing overstatement in the earlier phrase-based approach.
edges.evidence: Gentzkow-Shapiro (2010) scale media slant via partisan phrase frequencies; Gentzkow-Taddy (2019) show naive phrase-difference estimates are biased and apply a penalized multinomial-choice correction to Congressional speech.

edges.explanation: Provides an estimator for locating groups along a latent difference dimension from high-dimensional text choices, a methodological input to scaling political text.
edges.evidence: The paper quantifies partisan group differences in Congressional speech via a penalized multinomial model, the kind of measurement text-scaling tasks require.

edges.explanation: Both analyze US Congressional speech to recover partisan/positional signal, differing in method: bias-corrected choice modeling versus classification with agreement constraints.
edges.evidence: Thomas, Pang & Lee (2006) classify Congressional speeches by support/oppose using speaker relationships; Gentzkow-Taddy (2019) model phrase-choice differences across parties in the same domain.

edges.explanation: The survey explicitly distinguishes stance detection from sentiment analysis, grounding the concept that sentiment and stance are separate constructs.
edges.evidence: Küçük & Can dedicate discussion to the relationship and differences between stance detection and sentiment analysis, noting a target's stance need not match text polarity.

edges.explanation: Both are 2020 survey-type treatments of position/sentiment in text; one reviews stance detection generally while the other surveys sentiment and position-taking in parliamentary debate.
edges.evidence: Küçük & Can survey stance detection methods and datasets broadly; Abercrombie & Batista-Navarro (2020) survey sentiment and position analysis of political/parliamentary debate text.

edges.explanation: By delineating stance from sentiment and cataloguing methods for both, the survey informs sentiment-classification task design and its boundary with stance.
edges.evidence: The survey reviews sentiment analysis as a closely related task to stance detection and contrasts the two labeling objectives.

edges.explanation: This benchmark is a core dataset catalogued and analyzed by the stance-detection survey as a reference resource for the task.

edges.explanation: The benchmark provides stance-versus-sentiment annotations that support training and evaluating speech-level sentiment/stance classifiers.
edges.evidence: SemEval-2016 Task 6 releases tweets labeled for both stance toward a target and tweet sentiment, enabling analysis of the two tasks jointly.

edges.explanation: The task design separately annotates stance and sentiment, empirically demonstrating that the two labels diverge.
edges.evidence: Mohammad et al. provide both stance and sentiment labels and report that favorable stance does not coincide with positive sentiment, evidencing the distinction.

edges.explanation: IPSA is a parliamentary proceedings corpus and thus a member of the parliamentary-corpora family.

edges.evidence: IPSA provides OCR-digitised Italian plenary and committee material spanning 175 years, distinct from and not a substitute for a dedicated Camera XIX retrieval corpus.

edges.explanation: Both are single-country richly structured parliamentary corpora built from national legislative records.

edges.explanation: Both combine graph structure with QA-oriented retrieval/reasoning, making them comparable graph-based QA approaches.

edges.explanation: QA-GNN is a concrete KG-enhanced reasoning method of the kind the roadmap organises under LLM+KG synergy.

edges.explanation: The LLM+KG roadmap extends earlier KG surveys by adding the large-language-model dimension to KG representation, acquisition, and application.
edges.evidence: Pan et al. survey unifying LLMs and KGs, building on prior comprehensive KG surveys such as Ji et al. (2022).

edges.explanation: GraphRAG is an example of the LLM-augmented-KG / synergized direction the roadmap categorises.
edges.evidence: GraphRAG uses an LLM to extract an entity graph and summarise communities, an LLM+KG synergy of the kind framed by the roadmap.

edges.explanation: HippoRAG combines LLM-based extraction with graph retrieval, fitting the synergized LLM+KG frameworks the roadmap describes.
edges.evidence: HippoRAG builds and retrieves over an LLM-constructed knowledge graph, matching the LLM-augmented KG category in the roadmap.

edges.explanation: GraphRAG performs knowledge-graph construction via information extraction, an instance of the acquisition methods the survey reviews.
